courses.title: Swift & On-Device AI Engineering
courses.summary: Build private, responsive Apple-platform AI features with Swift concurrency, model lifecycle control, and graceful capability fallback.

modules.title: A Safe Swift Inference Runtime
modules.summary: Use value semantics, structured concurrency, actors, and package integrity to make local inference dependable.

lessons.title: Model State Has an Owner
lessons.summary: Separate immutable request values from shared mutable model resources.

contentBlocks.text: Ownership prevents invisible interference

Swift structs copy value semantics into clear request snapshots, while model weights, caches, and sessions are expensive shared resources. Give mutable inference state one owner and expose message-like operations instead of letting views mutate it directly.
A Sendable value can cross concurrency boundaries safely; that does not make a non-thread-safe native model session safe to call from many tasks.
Partition the runtime
items: Immutable prompt and generation options as values
Cancellation flowing from view task to inference

challenge.prompt: Assign ownership for a local model session
challenge.instructions: Explain why one actor should own a mutable key-value cache while request options remain ordinary Sendable structs.
challenge.explanation: The actor serializes mutation of cache state that belongs to a generation session, while independent immutable options can cross tasks without synchronization or accidental coupling.
hints: Identify which data changes during token generation.
Ask which values can be copied without changing behavior.
Separate UI observation from model mutation.

lessons.title: Make Generation Cancellable
lessons.summary: Use structured tasks so navigation and explicit stop actions release compute promptly.

contentBlocks.text: A disappeared screen should not keep decoding

Swift task cancellation is cooperative. The UI cancels its child task, but the generation loop must check cancellation between tokens or batches and unwind model resources without publishing stale results.
Detached tasks break the natural lifetime relationship. Use them only when work genuinely must outlive its caller and has another owner.

challenge.prompt: Stop work when a lesson closes
challenge.instructions: A learner starts generation, then leaves the screen. Which design best prevents hidden background inference?

choices.text: Run inference as a view-owned structured task and check cancellation in the decode loop.
Launch an untracked detached task for every request.
Ignore cancellation until the entire answer completes.

challenge.explanation: Structured task lifetime follows the view operation, and cooperative checks let the costly loop stop at a predictable boundary.
hints: Connect the task lifetime to the user-visible operation.
Cancellation must be observed by computation.

lessons.title: Build an Actor-Owned Model Cache
lessons.summary: Deduplicate concurrent loads and evict old models within a memory budget.

contentBlocks.text: Loading once is a concurrency invariant

Two simultaneous requests for the same model must await the same in-flight load rather than allocate weights twice. An actor can store both completed models and loading tasks, then remove failed tasks so a later attempt can recover.

if let model = loaded[id] { return model }
if let task = loading[id] { return try await task.value }
Cache responsibilities

challenge.instructions: Return a loaded model, otherwise await an existing task, otherwise create and record one. Remove the loading entry after completion.

testCases.input: two concurrent calls with the same id
testCases.expected: one Model.load task and the same returned model

testCases.input: a failed load followed by retry
testCases.expected: loading entry cleared and second load may proceed

challenge.explanation: Recording the task before awaiting lets later callers share it; clearing on both success and failure prevents stale in-flight state.
hints: Assign task under loading[id] before await.
Await task.value inside a do/catch.
Clear loading[id] on every exit path.

lessons.title: Design a Verifiable Model Package
lessons.summary: Bind weights, tokenizer, prompt format, license, and checksum into one compatible artifact.

contentBlocks.text: Weights alone are not a deployable model

Local inference depends on a matching tokenizer, architecture configuration, quantization metadata, special-token IDs, and chat template. A signed manifest should declare every file and hash before the runtime memory-maps any untrusted download.
Package manifest
Atomic installation means validating in a staging directory, then renaming the complete package into place so crashes never expose a half-installed model.

challenge.prompt: Roll out a downloadable local model safely
challenge.instructions: Choose the design that prevents corrupted or incompatible artifacts from becoming active.

choices.text: Download to staging, verify signed manifest and every hash, load-test compatibility, then atomically activate.
Stream bytes directly over the active model directory.
Trust the filename and skip tokenizer version checks.

challenge.explanation: Staged verification establishes integrity and compatibility before one atomic activation boundary, preserving the previous working package on failure.
hints: A download can stop between files.
Weights and tokenizer must describe the same vocabulary.
Preserve rollback until validation succeeds.

lessons.title: Coalesce Tokens for a Smooth UI
lessons.summary: Batch tiny decoder events into bounded text updates without losing cancellation or the final tail.

contentBlocks.text: Token rate and render rate are different
Publishing every token can trigger excessive main-thread layout. Accumulate pieces until a character threshold or time interval, yield one chunk, and always flush the remainder when generation ends.

buffer += piece
if buffer.count >= threshold { yield(buffer); buffer = "" }
Bound the AsyncStream buffering policy when consumers may be slower than producers; otherwise queued UI updates can grow without limit.

challenge.instructions: Append pieces, emit and clear at threshold, then emit any remaining tail.
challenge.explanation: The threshold limits update frequency, clearing starts the next chunk, and the final flush preserves text below the threshold.
hints: Append each piece to buffer first.
Clear buffer after appending a chunk.
Append a nonempty buffer after the loop.

modules.title: Device-Aware Intelligence
modules.summary: Route across built-in and downloaded models while controlling memory, retrieval, privacy, and fallback UX.

lessons.title: Treat Inference as a Device Lifecycle
lessons.summary: Plan cold start, prewarm, foreground pressure, thermal throttling, and background suspension.

contentBlocks.text: Local does not mean free

On-device models compete with the interface and other apps for unified memory, power, and thermal headroom. Prewarm only when intent is strong, release recoverable caches under pressure, and checkpoint long work before the app may suspend.
Measure by device class
items: Cold and warm time to first token

contentBlocks.text: Simulator benchmarks do not predict neural-engine, GPU, or memory behavior on physical devices; maintain a representative hardware matrix.

challenge.instructions: Describe when a tutor app should begin loading a local model and when it should release optional caches.
challenge.explanation: Prewarm after a strong signal such as opening Tutor or focusing the composer, not at every app launch; release regenerable caches on memory pressure, prolonged inactivity, or thermal constraint.
hints: Balance first-token latency against unused work.
Separate persistent weights from regenerable session cache.
Use user intent and device signals.

lessons.title: Map Runtime Availability to UX
lessons.summary: Convert device and package states into actionable, nonmisleading tutor status.

contentBlocks.text: Unavailable has several causes

A built-in model may be unsupported, disabled, not ready, or temporarily busy; a downloadable model may be absent, verifying, or incompatible. Preserve these distinctions so the interface can offer the correct recovery rather than a generic error.
Never label a remote fallback as offline. The selected engine, privacy boundary, and likely data path must remain visible.

challenge.prompt: Map engine status to a recovery action
challenge.instructions: Return useLocal, offerDownload, or useFallback for ready, missing, and every other state.
challenge.explanation: The mapping preserves the only user-fixable package state while ensuring unsupported or disabled devices retain a functional fallback.
hints: Ready selects useLocal.
Only missing should prompt download.
Use the fallback for remaining states.

lessons.title: Pack Local Evidence within Token Limits
lessons.summary: Select diverse curriculum passages without exceeding a small on-device context budget.

contentBlocks.text: Small models need sharper context

Local tutors benefit from retrieving concise, source-labeled curriculum blocks. Select high-score passages, reject duplicate lesson IDs when diversity matters, and reserve output capacity before packing any evidence.

guard used + item.tokens <= budget else { continue }
guard !seenLessons.contains(item.lessonID) else { continue }
Token estimates must use the active model tokenizer when hard limits matter; character heuristics need a safety margin.

challenge.instructions: Walk score-sorted candidates, keep at most one per lesson, and never exceed budget.

testCases.input: two top items from one lesson plus a lower distinct lesson
testCases.expected: one top item and the distinct lesson
candidate omitted and total tokens within budget

challenge.explanation: Score ordering preserves relevance, the seen set enforces lesson diversity, and used tokens maintain the hard packing invariant.
hints: First reject a lesson already in seen.
Check used + item.tokens against budget.
Increment used only after selection.

lessons.title: Route across Offline Engines
lessons.summary: Select a built-in model, downloaded model, or deterministic knowledge tutor without lying about capability.

contentBlocks.text: Automatic routing needs an explainable policy

Prefer an available on-device generative model for open explanations, a smaller downloaded model for supported hardware, and a deterministic retrieval tutor everywhere. User selection, task capability, memory headroom, and offline requirement should outrank novelty.
Routing inputs
Fallback should preserve function at reduced capability and say so: a curriculum-grounded explainer is different from an unrestricted generative tutor.

challenge.instructions: The built-in model is unavailable and no model pack is installed. What should automatic mode do?

choices.text: Use the bundled retrieval-and-explanation tutor and visibly label its capability.
Silently send the question to an external API.
Pretend a generative model answered while returning canned text.

challenge.explanation: The deterministic local tutor preserves offline function and an honest capability boundary without requiring accounts or transmitting learner data.
hints: Offline is a hard user constraint.
A fallback can be narrower and still useful.
Make engine identity visible.

lessons.title: Verify the Offline Privacy Boundary
lessons.summary: Test that local mode performs no network transfer and stores sensitive context minimally.

contentBlocks.text: Privacy claims need observable evidence

Offline mode should function with networking disabled, avoid analytics payloads containing prompts, and keep transcripts under clear retention controls. Network-framework tests and packet inspection can verify that a code path never opens a connection.
Privacy test matrix
Downloading an optional model is a network event; distinguish installation-time transfer from inference-time offline operation.

challenge.instructions: Which evidence most directly supports the claim?

choices.text: Automated tests pass with network denied, and packet capture shows no inference-time connections.
The settings screen uses a cloud icon with a slash.
A developer remembers not adding an API call.

challenge.explanation: Behavioral tests under enforced network denial and independent traffic observation verify the running product, including accidental dependencies.
hints: A claim should survive a hostile test environment.
Inspect actual network behavior, not only interface text.

courses.title: Advanced RAG & Knowledge Systems
courses.summary: Engineer multi-stage retrieval over versioned, permissioned corpora with reranking, graph context, and evidence-level evaluation.

modules.title: The Retrieval Funnel
modules.summary: Preserve corpus provenance while expanding queries, recovering parent context, and fusing rankers.

lessons.title: A Knowledge Corpus Is a Versioned Product
lessons.summary: Bind every retrievable passage to source identity, parser version, and effective time.

contentBlocks.text: Answers inherit the quality of ingestion

Advanced retrieval begins before embeddings. Each chunk needs stable source and parent IDs, byte or page location, content hash, parser version, access labels, and validity interval so citations can be reconstructed and stale knowledge withdrawn.
Lineage questions
items: Which immutable source produced this text?
When did the fact become effective?

contentBlocks.text: A re-index that changes chunk boundaries without preserving source anchors can invalidate stored citations even when document text is unchanged.

challenge.instructions: Describe the fields needed to trace a result through a parser upgrade and back to the original page.
challenge.explanation: Use stable document identity plus version, source location, content hash, parser version, and chunk revision; keep index generation separately so retrieval runs can be reproduced.
hints: A list position changes after rechunking.
Preserve both source location and transformation identity.
Separate document version from index version.

lessons.title: Expand Queries without Drifting
lessons.summary: Use multiple search formulations while guarding the original intent and constraints.

contentBlocks.text: Recall gains can introduce semantic drift

Multi-query retrieval generates paraphrases or subquestions to recover differently worded evidence. Each expansion should preserve named entities, dates, negation, and jurisdiction; otherwise a broader query can retrieve plausible but inapplicable material.

original: EU retention rule after 2025
expansion: European Union data-retention requirement effective after 2025
Keep the original query in the candidate union and score expansions for constraint preservation before they influence retrieval.

challenge.instructions: The original asks for policies that do not allow storage. Which expansion is unsafe?

choices.text: policies that prohibit retaining user data
policies that allow storage of user data
data-retention bans and no-storage requirements

challenge.explanation: It drops the negation and reverses the requested constraint, so its candidates can pull the retrieval set toward the opposite policy.
hints: Track the word "not" semantically.
Compare whether each version permits or forbids storage.

lessons.title: Retrieve Children, Return Parents
lessons.summary: Search focused child chunks while returning deduplicated parent sections for complete context.

contentBlocks.text: Match narrowly, explain broadly

Small child chunks improve semantic matching, but answers may require their surrounding definition or procedure. Parent-child retrieval ranks children, maps hits to parent IDs, then returns each parent once in best-hit order.
Cap parent size and preserve the matched child anchor; a giant parent can erase the context-efficiency benefit.

challenge.instructions: Map child hits to parents, preserving first-hit order and returning each parent once.
challenge.explanation: The first child hit determines each parent’s rank, while the seen set prevents repeated surrounding sections.
hints: Skip when parent_id is already in seen.
Add the ID before appending its parent.
Do not sort parents again.

lessons.title: Place a Cross-Encoder Reranker
lessons.summary: Spend expensive joint query-document scoring only after high-recall candidate retrieval.

contentBlocks.text: Bi-encoders retrieve; cross-encoders discriminate

Vector search precomputes document embeddings and scales well. A cross-encoder reads query and candidate together, capturing fine interactions but costing one forward pass per pair. Use it on a bounded candidate set with deadlines and batching.
Tune the funnel
items: Pairs per query and batch size

contentBlocks.text: A reranker cannot recover evidence absent from candidates. Diagnose candidate recall before replacing the reranker.

challenge.instructions: Vector search returns 200 candidates, but reranking all exceeds the deadline. Choose a defensible plan.

choices.text: Tune first-stage retrieval to preserve recall in a smaller pool, batch rerank it, and retain a score-only fallback.
Rerank the entire corpus for every query.
Drop the deadline and let requests queue indefinitely.

challenge.explanation: The plan treats candidate size as a measured quality-latency parameter and preserves service under reranker timeout.
hints: Reduce pairs without blindly discarding recall.
Batching improves accelerator utilization.
Define behavior when the stronger stage misses its budget.

lessons.title: Fuse Rankings without Score Calibration
lessons.summary: Implement reciprocal-rank fusion across lexical, dense, and specialized retrievers.

contentBlocks.text: Ranks are easier to combine than unrelated scores
Reciprocal-rank fusion adds 1/(k + rank) for each appearance of a document. It rewards items supported by multiple retrievers without assuming BM25 and cosine scores share a meaningful numeric scale.

fused[doc_id] += 1.0 / (offset + rank)
# rank starts at 1
The offset controls how much top positions dominate. Tune it and retriever weights on labeled queries rather than copying a constant blindly.

challenge.instructions: Accumulate reciprocal rank by document ID and return IDs ordered by descending fused score.

testCases.expected: b ranks first because both lists support it

challenge.explanation: Every occurrence contributes by rank, and deterministic ID tie-breaking stabilizes equally scored documents.
hints: Add 1.0 divided by offset plus rank.
Sort on negative score for descending order.
Use document ID as a stable tie-breaker.

modules.title: Structured and Temporal Knowledge
modules.summary: Join vector evidence with entity links, graph facts, time validity, permissions, and grounded test sets.

lessons.title: Graphs and Vectors Answer Different Questions
lessons.summary: Use vector search for fuzzy meaning and graph traversal for explicit relationships.

contentBlocks.text: Similarity is not a relationship database

Embeddings retrieve passages that resemble a question. A knowledge graph represents typed entities and edges such as service OWNS dataset or policy SUPERSEDES version. Hybrid systems use semantic search to find evidence and graph traversal to constrain or expand explicit relationships.
Choose the representation
items: Free text supporting an edge → source passage

contentBlocks.text: Every graph assertion needs provenance and validity. A precise edge without source or effective date can be confidently stale.

challenge.instructions: For "Which customer features depend on dataset X, and why?", describe how graph and vector retrieval cooperate.
challenge.explanation: Traverse explicit DEPENDS_ON edges from dataset X to features, then retrieve source passages attached to those edges or entities to explain the dependency with evidence.
hints: One part asks for exact connected objects.
The word "why" needs supporting prose.
Return graph facts with source citations.

lessons.title: Resolve Mentions to Canonical Entities
lessons.summary: Combine normalized aliases and context scores while preserving an unresolved state.

contentBlocks.text: A name is not an identity

Aliases, abbreviations, and duplicate names make entity linking probabilistic. Generate candidates from normalized aliases, rerank using type and surrounding context, and require a margin over the runner-up before attaching a canonical ID.

if best.score < threshold or best.score - second.score < margin:
    return None
An unresolved mention is safer than a wrong high-impact link. Store the mention span and candidates for later correction.

challenge.instructions: Return the best entity ID only when its score meets threshold and beats second place by margin.
challenge.explanation: Absolute confidence rejects weak candidates, while the margin rejects ambiguous competitions even when both scores are high.
hints: Subtract second_score from the best score.
Reject when that difference is below margin.
Return ordered[0] only after both gates.

lessons.title: Filter Knowledge by Effective Time
lessons.summary: Select facts valid at the question’s time rather than blindly using the latest record.

contentBlocks.text: Current and historically correct are different

A temporal fact has a valid-from boundary and an optional valid-until boundary. A historical question must filter by the requested instant before ranking; current-only indexing would erase the evidence needed to answer past-state questions.
valid = fact.valid_from <= at and (fact.valid_until is None or at < fact.valid_until)
Use half-open intervals [from, until) so adjacent versions do not both appear valid at the exact transition time.

challenge.prompt: Select facts valid at an instant
challenge.instructions: Return facts where valid_from <= at and valid_until is absent or strictly after at.
challenge.explanation: The half-open interval includes its start and excludes its end, producing one unambiguous active version at transitions.
hints: No valid_until means still active.
Use at < until, not <=.
Require both started and not_ended.

lessons.title: Make Authorization Part of Retrieval
lessons.summary: Apply identity-derived filters before candidate material enters reranking, logs, or model context.

contentBlocks.text: Post-filtering can already be a leak

If unauthorized chunks are retrieved and then discarded, their text or metadata may still appear in traces, caches, or reranker inputs. Push tenant and document ACL constraints into the earliest storage query and recheck access when dereferencing results.
Defense in depth
items: Audit logs record policy decision IDs

contentBlocks.text: Never accept an allowlist from prompt text. Authorization context must be constructed by trusted application code.

challenge.instructions: Choose a query-cache key for results that depend on user groups.

choices.text: Normalized query, index version, and a stable authorization-scope hash.
Normalized query alone, shared by every tenant.
The model-generated answer text only.

challenge.explanation: Including the effective authorization scope prevents results retrieved for one permission set from being served to another.
hints: Identical questions can have different permitted evidence.
The key needs data and policy versioning.
Avoid raw sensitive group lists when a stable hash suffices.

lessons.title: Score Evidence Coverage and Support
lessons.summary: Evaluate whether retrieved passages cover required facts and whether citations entail answer claims.

contentBlocks.text: Relevance is necessary but not sufficient

Evidence coverage asks whether sources contain every required answer fact. Citation precision asks whether each cited passage supports its attached claim. Include counterfactual, conflicting-source, stale-version, and unanswerable cases.
Evaluation layers
An answer can be fully faithful to incomplete context and still be wrong by omission; coverage and faithfulness must be reported separately.

challenge.prompt: Diagnose a supported but incomplete answer
challenge.instructions: Every sentence cites supporting evidence, but one required policy exception is absent from both context and answer. Which metric exposes the primary failure?

choices.text: Evidence coverage over required facts
Citation formatting validity alone
Generation token count

challenge.explanation: Citation support is strong for included claims, but coverage reveals the missing exception that retrieval or context assembly failed to supply.
hints: Distinguish unsupported claims from missing claims.
The absent fact never reached generation.

courses.title: Agent Protocols & Multi-Agent Systems
courses.summary: Design bounded agent loops, typed tool protocols, durable handoffs, multi-agent budgets, and evaluations that expose coordination failures.

modules.title: Bounded Agent Contracts
modules.summary: Turn model-directed tool use into a state machine with validated effects and durable recovery.

lessons.title: An Agent Is a Controlled Loop
lessons.summary: Model observation, decision, action, and updated state as explicit transitions.

contentBlocks.text: Agency comes from the runtime, not a prompt

An agent runtime presents state and available actions, asks a model for a proposal, validates it, executes through tools, records the result, and decides whether to continue. Step, time, token, cost, and permission limits bound the loop.
Every step records
A text response claiming completion is not proof. Completion should depend on verifiable state or an explicit terminal tool result.

challenge.instructions: For an agent that prepares a deployment but may not publish it, describe a verifiable stopping state.
challenge.explanation: Stop when a validated deployment plan artifact and passing preflight results are stored, with publish permission still absent; do not equate a model statement with executed deployment.
hints: Name an observable artifact.
Respect the agent’s authorization boundary.
Separate preparing from publishing.

lessons.title: Tools Are Typed Capabilities
lessons.summary: Define narrow actions with semantic validation and explicit error categories.

contentBlocks.text: A schema describes shape, not permission

A tool contract names one capability, documents fields, constrains types and enums, and returns structured results. Trusted code still checks current authorization, resource existence, state version, and business invariants before effects.
{"action":"schedule_job","dataset_id":"ds_42","run_at":"2027-01-02T09:00Z"}
Avoid one universal execute(command: string) tool. Narrow capabilities reduce prompt-injection blast radius and make policy review tractable.

challenge.instructions: An agent only needs to read test status and create a draft release note. Which tool set is strongest?

choices.text: get_test_status and create_draft_release_note with typed fields
run_any_shell_command as administrator
publish_release with no approval argument

challenge.explanation: The two typed tools exactly match required capabilities without granting unrelated execution or publication authority.
hints: List only actions the task requires.
Draft creation is different from publication.

lessons.title: Validate Tool Calls before Dispatch
lessons.summary: Check allowlists, argument requirements, and expected state version before invocation.

contentBlocks.text: Dispatch is a security boundary

Parsing a tool call only proves syntactic structure. The dispatcher must confirm the tool is allowed for this agent, required arguments exist, resource scope is authorized, and optimistic state versions still match.

if call.name not in allowed: reject("tool_not_allowed")
if call.version != current_version: reject("stale_state")
Return machine-readable rejection codes to the loop, but do not expose sensitive policy internals that help an attacker probe access.

challenge.instructions: Return error codes for disallowed tools, missing required arguments, or stale version; otherwise return ok.

testCases.input: allowed complete call with old version

challenge.explanation: The ordered gates reject capability, structure, and concurrency defects before any effectful code receives the proposal.
hints: Look for field inside call arguments.
Compare the proposal version with current_version.
Do not dispatch on any non-ok result.

lessons.title: Design a Durable Agent Handoff
lessons.summary: Transfer bounded work through a typed artifact rather than an ambiguous conversational summary.

contentBlocks.text: A handoff is a protocol transition

The sending agent should emit objective, completed evidence, remaining work, constraints, artifact references, budget, and requested receiver capability. The orchestrator validates the packet and chooses a receiver; agents should not invent unregistered peers.
Handoff packet
Use durable storage for large artifacts and pass references with checksums. Copying full context between agents increases cost and creates inconsistent duplicates.

challenge.prompt: Handoff a failed data validation task
challenge.instructions: Choose the packet that lets a specialist continue without repeating or trusting unsupported claims.

choices.text: Dataset version, validator report URI and hash, exact failing rules, attempted fixes, acceptance criteria, and remaining budget.
A message saying "data is weird, please fix".
The entire unbounded conversation with no objective.

challenge.explanation: It transfers reproducible evidence, explicit remaining work, and integrity-checked artifacts while preserving bounded scope.
hints: The receiver needs to reproduce the failure.
Claims should link to evidence.
Keep the acceptance condition explicit.

lessons.title: Make Retried Actions Idempotent
lessons.summary: Use an operation key so network retries return the original result instead of duplicating effects.

contentBlocks.text: At-least-once delivery must not mean repeated side effects
A timeout may occur after a tool committed but before the agent received confirmation. Store an idempotency key and result atomically with the effect; a retry with the same key returns that result.

if key in operations: return operations[key]
result = perform_once()
operations[key] = result
Bind the key to an argument hash. Reusing one key with different arguments is a conflict, not a cache hit.

challenge.instructions: Return stored result for a matching key and argument hash; reject key reuse with changed arguments.

testCases.input: same key and hash called twice
testCases.expected: perform called once and identical result returned

challenge.explanation: The persisted argument hash distinguishes a legitimate delivery retry from accidental or malicious reuse for another operation.
hints: Return existing result after the hash matches.
Store both hash and result on first execution.
Return the newly performed result.

modules.title: Multi-Agent Coordination Runtime
modules.summary: Specialize agents behind an orchestrator that budgets work, validates messages, and measures coordination overhead.

lessons.title: Specialize around Information and Tools
lessons.summary: Create another agent only when its bounded context or capability materially improves the task.

contentBlocks.text: More agents are not automatically more intelligence

A specialist earns its place through distinct tools, data access, evaluation criteria, or a parallelizable work unit. Excessive decomposition adds handoff loss, duplicated context, latency, and conflicts that one capable agent might avoid.
Good specialization boundaries
Measure total quality per token and elapsed second against a single-agent baseline; coordination is an engineering hypothesis, not a virtue.

challenge.instructions: A second agent would receive the same tools, context, and sequential task as the first. Explain the likely trade-off.
challenge.explanation: It adds context transfer and coordination without distinct capability or parallelism, so a single agent is probably simpler and cheaper unless evaluation demonstrates a quality gain.
hints: Ask what unique resource the second agent contributes.
Sequential dependency blocks parallel speedup.
Compare against a baseline.

lessons.title: Validate an Agent Message Envelope
lessons.summary: Reject expired, misrouted, or duplicate inter-agent messages before processing payloads.

contentBlocks.text: Messages need identity and lifetime

An envelope should include message, trace, sender, recipient, schema version, creation and expiry times, and payload hash. Recipients deduplicate message IDs and reject expired or incorrectly addressed work.

if envelope.id in seen: return "duplicate"
if now >= envelope.expires_at: return "expired"
Authenticate the sender at the transport layer. A sender field inside an unsigned payload is merely a claim.

challenge.instructions: Return duplicate, wrong_recipient, expired, or accepted; add accepted IDs to seen.

testCases.expected: accepted and ID added to seen

challenge.explanation: The receiver validates envelope invariants before accepting ownership and records identity to make repeated delivery harmless.
hints: Return wrong_recipient on address mismatch.
Expiry is reached when now is greater than or equal.
Add ID only for accepted messages.

lessons.title: Allocate a Shared Agent Budget
lessons.summary: Reserve token and time budgets atomically so parallel agents cannot overspend a common ceiling.

contentBlocks.text: Parallel work shares finite resources

The orchestrator should reserve budget before spawning or calling a worker, then reconcile unused capacity on completion. Atomic reservation prevents two simultaneous decisions from each seeing the same remaining budget.

if request > ledger.remaining: return False
ledger.remaining -= request
ledger.reservations[worker] = request
Budget exhaustion should produce a partial-evidence result, not pressure agents to fabricate completion.

challenge.instructions: Reserve only when enough remains; on completion return unused units and remove the reservation.
challenge.explanation: Pre-decrement makes the commitment visible to other workers; reconciliation restores only genuinely unused capacity.
hints: Store units under the worker key.
Unused is reserved minus used, bounded below by zero.
pop removes completed reservation.

lessons.title: Choose a Coordination Topology
lessons.summary: Match central orchestration, pipelines, and limited peer exchange to dependency and risk.

contentBlocks.text: Topology determines control and failure propagation

A central orchestrator simplifies budgets, permissions, and termination. A pipeline fits ordered transformations. Peer debate can diversify analysis but needs strict turn, message, and consensus limits to prevent loops and collusion.
Topology criteria
Do not let agents recursively spawn unbounded peers. The orchestrator should own the registered topology and maximum depth.

challenge.prompt: Coordinate parallel research and one final decision
challenge.instructions: Three specialists independently inspect evidence, then one policy owner must choose. Which topology is clearest?

choices.text: Central orchestrator fans out bounded research, validates artifacts, then routes them to the authorized policy owner.
Every agent spawns more agents until they agree.
Allow the fastest specialist to execute the decision regardless of permission.

challenge.explanation: Fan-out gains parallel evidence collection while central aggregation preserves budget, traceability, and the final authority boundary.
hints: Research is parallel; decision is singular.
The final actor has distinct authorization.
Keep the spawn graph bounded.

lessons.title: Evaluate the Team, Not Just the Answer
lessons.summary: Measure task success together with handoff loss, duplicated work, budget use, and unsafe actions.

contentBlocks.text: A good final answer can hide a fragile process

Agent evaluation should replay full traces and label unnecessary tool calls, repeated searches, lost constraints, unauthorized attempts, unverified completion, and communication overhead. Compare against simpler topologies on matched tasks.
Team metrics
Evaluate perturbations: delayed messages, tool timeouts, one incorrect specialist, and budget pressure reveal whether coordination degrades safely.

challenge.instructions: A team gains 1% task success but uses 6× tokens and doubles unsafe tool proposals. What is the sound conclusion?

choices.text: The topology is not justified yet; investigate or simplify given cost and safety regression.
More agents are always better, so ship it.
Ignore process metrics because the final score rose.

challenge.explanation: A marginal quality gain does not automatically outweigh large efficiency and safety regressions; deployment requires an explicit utility threshold.
hints: Compare all objectives, not only one score.
Unsafe proposals impose review and incident risk.

courses.title: Realtime Voice AI
courses.summary: Build low-latency spoken agents with streaming audio, turn detection, interruption, partial hypotheses, and end-to-end conversational evaluation.

modules.title: Realtime Audio Transport
modules.summary: Budget latency, frame speech, smooth network jitter, and maintain revisable transcripts.

lessons.title: Budget the Mouth-to-Ear Path
lessons.summary: Decompose conversational delay across capture, transport, inference, and playback.

contentBlocks.text: Voice latency is the sum of a pipeline

Perceived response time includes audio framing, network transit, turn detection, speech recognition, reasoning, first synthesized audio, jitter buffering, and device playback. Instrument timestamps at each boundary instead of blaming one model.
Track distinct milestones
Streaming can lower time to first audio while total completion stays unchanged; measure both responsiveness and full-turn duration.

challenge.instructions: Turn detection consumes 900 ms while every other stage totals 450 ms. Identify the first experiment.
challenge.explanation: Tune or adapt end-of-turn detection and measure interruption rate, because it dominates current latency; do not replace the language model before testing the actual bottleneck.
hints: Compare stage durations numerically.
Reducing silence wait may increase premature turns.
Measure quality and latency together.

lessons.title: Choose an Audio Frame Size
lessons.summary: Balance packet overhead, scheduling frequency, and algorithmic latency.

contentBlocks.text: Frames set the processing cadence

Short frames reach detectors quickly but create more packets and callbacks. Long frames improve batching efficiency but withhold audio longer. Speech systems often begin around tens of milliseconds and benchmark on target networks and devices.

samples_per_frame = sample_rate * frame_ms / 1000
# 16 kHz × 20 ms = 320 samples
Codec packetization, echo cancellation, and VAD may require specific frame sizes; align boundaries instead of repeatedly copying audio.

challenge.instructions: At 16,000 samples/second, how many samples are in a 20 ms mono frame?
challenge.explanation: Twenty milliseconds is 0.02 seconds, and 16,000 × 0.02 = 320 samples.
hints: Convert milliseconds to seconds.
Multiply sample rate by frame duration.

lessons.title: Reorder a Small Jitter Window
lessons.summary: Emit network audio frames in sequence while buffering limited out-of-order arrival.

contentBlocks.text: Networks deliver timing variation, not a metronome

A jitter buffer holds frames briefly so late packets can be reordered. It emits contiguous sequence numbers, drops duplicates, and declares a loss when waiting beyond its latency budget rather than stalling playback forever.
A larger buffer conceals more jitter but adds mouth-to-ear latency. Adapt its target from observed delay variation with strict bounds.

challenge.instructions: Insert a frame unless old or duplicate, then emit every now-contiguous sequence from expected.

testCases.expected: first emits none; second emits frames 1 and 2

challenge.explanation: Pending storage absorbs reordering, and the loop releases only a gap-free prefix so playback order remains correct.
hints: Continue while expected is a key in pending.
Increment expected after each emitted frame.
Do not emit frame 2 while frame 1 is absent.

lessons.title: Combine VAD with Semantic Turn Signals
lessons.summary: Avoid both long silence waits and premature interruption of thoughtful speakers.

contentBlocks.text: Silence is evidence, not certainty

Voice activity detection separates speech-like audio from silence, but a pause may occur inside a turn. Combine acoustic duration, transcript completeness, discourse cues, user-specific pace, and an explicit push-to-talk or done control.
Adaptive endpointing signals
Optimize a cost curve: faster endpointing lowers latency but raises false endpoints that damage trust and force repair turns.

challenge.prompt: Serve a speaker with frequent mid-sentence pauses
challenge.instructions: Choose the best endpoint policy adaptation.

choices.text: Increase patience when transcript syntax appears incomplete, while retaining a maximum deadline and manual done control.
End every turn after the same 200 ms silence.
Disable turn completion entirely.

challenge.explanation: It uses semantic evidence and observed speaking style to reduce interruptions without allowing unbounded silence.
hints: A pause does not always close a sentence.
Keep an upper latency bound.
Give users an explicit override.

lessons.title: Merge Partial Transcript Revisions
lessons.summary: Replace unstable recognition suffixes while preserving committed text.

contentBlocks.text: Partial ASR output is a hypothesis

Streaming recognizers often mark a stable prefix and revise the remaining suffix as more audio arrives. Store committed and unstable text separately; never trigger irreversible tools from an unfinalized hypothesis.

display = committed + partial
if update.is_final: committed += update.text; partial = ""
Use segment IDs or time ranges to reject late updates from an earlier utterance after a reconnect.

challenge.prompt: Apply partial and final transcript updates
challenge.instructions: Replace partial text on interim updates; append to committed and clear partial on final updates.
challenge.explanation: Interim hypotheses replace the unstable suffix, while final text becomes immutable history for the current utterance.
hints: Clear partial after committing final text.
Assign rather than append interim text.
Build display from both state fields.

modules.title: Conversation Control and Quality
modules.summary: Synchronize multimodal state, support barge-in, trace timing, and test noisy real-world conversations.

lessons.title: Model Full-Duplex Conversation State
lessons.summary: Represent listening, thinking, speaking, interrupted, and recovering as explicit states.

contentBlocks.text: Audio input and output can overlap
A full-duplex agent may hear the user while speaking. Explicit states and events prevent races between playback completion, new speech, network reconnect, cancellation, and a late model token stream.
Important events
Attach a monotonically increasing turn ID to every transcript, model, and audio event so late work cannot mutate the current turn.

challenge.instructions: Turn 7 is interrupted and turn 8 begins; then playbackDrained for turn 7 arrives. Explain the state guard.
challenge.explanation: Ignore the event when its turn ID is not the active output turn; otherwise it could incorrectly mark turn 8 as finished or change listening state.
hints: Asynchronous events can arrive out of order.
Identity is safer than relying on timing.
State transitions should validate their source turn.

lessons.title: Cancel Speech on Barge-In
lessons.summary: Stop queued audio, cancel generation, and retain only what the user actually heard.

contentBlocks.text: Interruption crosses three subsystems

When user speech begins during playback, stop the audio device, discard queued synthesized chunks, cancel upstream generation, and mark the assistant transcript at the last audible offset—not the last generated token.

playback.stop(); queue.clear(); generation.cancel()
assistant_turn.truncate(at: last_audible_character)
Echo cancellation must distinguish the device’s own audio from actual barge-in or the agent may repeatedly interrupt itself.

challenge.instructions: For the active turn, cancel generation, clear audio queue, and truncate displayed text to audible characters.
challenge.starterCode:
def barge_in(state, turn_id, audible_characters):
    if state["active_turn"] != turn_id:
        return False
    state["generation_cancelled"] = True
    ____
    state["assistant_text"] = ____
    state["mode"] = "listening"
    return True
challenge.solution:
def barge_in(state, turn_id, audible_characters):
    if state["active_turn"] != turn_id:
        return False
    state["generation_cancelled"] = True
    state["audio_queue"].clear()
    state["assistant_text"] = state["assistant_text"][:audible_characters]
    state["mode"] = "listening"
    return True

testCases.input: active turn with 20 chars generated and 8 audible
testCases.expected: queue empty, text first 8 chars, mode listening

challenge.explanation: The turn guard blocks stale events, and truncating to audible progress keeps conversation history aligned with user experience.
hints: Clear the audio_queue collection.
Slice assistant_text at audible_characters.
Do nothing for a non-active turn.

lessons.title: Compute Stage Latencies from Trace Events
lessons.summary: Derive turn-detection, reasoning, and first-audio delays from monotonic timestamps.

contentBlocks.text: One trace turns "slow" into a repair target
Use a monotonic clock for durations so wall-clock adjustments cannot create negative latency. Store named events under one turn ID and compute only intervals whose endpoints exist.

endpoint_delay = turn_committed - speech_ended
first_audio_delay = audio_started - turn_committed
Report percentiles by device, network, language, and interruption state; averages conceal tail conversations that feel broken.

challenge.instructions: Return endpoint and response delays when their timestamp pairs exist; omit unavailable metrics.
challenge.explanation: Named endpoint subtraction isolates distinct delays, and presence guards avoid manufacturing values from incomplete traces.
hints: Later timestamp minus earlier timestamp.
First audio is measured from committed turn.
Do not insert a metric without both events.

lessons.title: Minimize Voice Data Retention
lessons.summary: Separate transient audio transport from consented recording, transcripts, and debugging samples.

contentBlocks.text: A voice stream contains more than words

Audio may reveal identity, environment, health, and bystanders. Process frames ephemerally by default, disclose recording state, encrypt transport, apply short explicit retention, and require separate consent for training or human review.
Data classes need separate controls
A transcript deletion request must also remove search indexes, caches, and derived user memory tied to it, not only the visible chat row.

challenge.prompt: Debug recognition without retaining every call
challenge.instructions: Choose a privacy-preserving data strategy.

choices.text: Opt-in sampled clips with redaction, short retention, strict reviewer access, and aggregate metrics for all other traffic.
Store every raw conversation indefinitely because it may help someday.
Hide recording in the terms while showing no in-call indicator.

challenge.explanation: It limits collection and access while preserving a consented, auditable sample for targeted quality analysis.
hints: Collect the minimum needed for the stated purpose.
Make consent and recording state visible.
Use aggregate telemetry when raw content is unnecessary.

lessons.title: Evaluate Conversation under Noise and Interruption
lessons.summary: Measure task success, timing, recognition, prosody, and repair over complete spoken turns.

contentBlocks.text: Text-only evaluation misses the voice product

A useful suite includes accents, code-switching, background speech, packet loss, echo, long pauses, barge-in, corrections, and emotionally sensitive pacing. Score semantic task success alongside endpoint errors and response latency.
Voice-system outcomes
Replayable recorded scenarios support regression testing, but live network and hardware sessions are still needed for echo and device timing.

challenge.instructions: Recognition is accurate, but users complain the assistant constantly talks over them. What evaluation is missing?

choices.text: Turn-taking, false endpoint, and barge-in behavior.
Only a larger language-model benchmark.
Image classification accuracy.

challenge.explanation: Transcription quality can be strong while endpointing and interruption control make conversation unusable; those interaction metrics target the complaint.
hints: The words are correct, but timing is wrong.
Evaluate who has the floor and how quickly playback stops.

courses.title: Computer Vision Engineering
courses.summary: Build image classification and detection systems with reliable geometry, data augmentation, post-processing, deployment, and slice-aware evaluation.

modules.title: Pixels, Geometry, and Models
modules.summary: Preserve image meaning through preprocessing, augmentation, box metrics, architecture selection, and suppression.

lessons.title: An Image Tensor Has a Coordinate Contract
lessons.summary: Track axis order, color space, range, and spatial transforms as model inputs.

contentBlocks.text: The same pixels can become different numbers

A model may expect RGB channels, floating values in 0–1, per-channel normalization, and NCHW axis order. Camera buffers may arrive as YUV or BGRA with rotation metadata. One explicit preprocessing contract prevents silent color and shape corruption.
Record for every tensor
items: Resize, crop, pad, and rotation transform

contentBlocks.text: Visualize the tensor after preprocessing and invert plotted boxes back onto the source image; this catches errors metrics can obscure.

challenge.instructions: A model trained on RGB receives BGR images and loses accuracy. Explain why dimensions alone did not catch the defect.
challenge.explanation: Both representations have three identically sized channels, but red and blue values exchange semantic positions, violating the learned input contract without a shape error.
hints: Shape describes size, not channel meaning.
Weights associate features with fixed channel positions.
Inspect a preprocessed image visually.

lessons.title: Transform Labels with Pixels
lessons.summary: Keep boxes, masks, and keypoints geometrically aligned through augmentation.

contentBlocks.text: Spatial augmentation changes the target

Brightness changes leave box geometry intact, but crops, flips, rotations, and perspective transforms move labels. Boxes need clipping and visibility rules; keypoints may swap semantic names under reflection.

horizontal flip: x_min' = width - x_max
                 x_max' = width - x_min
Augmentations should resemble plausible deployment variation. Unrealistic transformations can teach invariance to features the task actually needs.

challenge.instructions: A horizontal flip is applied to an image with left-eye and right-eye keypoints. What must happen?

choices.text: Transform coordinates and swap the semantic left/right keypoint labels.
Flip pixels while leaving every keypoint unchanged.
Delete all labels after augmentation.

challenge.explanation: Coordinates move geometrically, and anatomical label identity swaps relative to the image under reflection.
hints: Pixels and annotations must remain aligned.
A reflected left eye appears on the opposite image side.

lessons.title: Compute Bounding-Box IoU
lessons.summary: Measure overlap using intersection area divided by union area with non-overlap guards.

contentBlocks.text: Intersection over union normalizes overlap
For boxes [x1, y1, x2, y2], intersect the maximum left/top with minimum right/bottom. Clamp negative intersection width or height to zero. Union equals both areas minus their intersection.

intersection = max(0, right-left) * max(0, bottom-top)
union = area_a + area_b - intersection
Coordinate conventions matter: continuous coordinates and inclusive pixel indices use different width formulas. Choose one contract and test edge-touching boxes.

challenge.instructions: Return zero for no union; otherwise intersection divided by union.
challenge.starterCode:
def iou(a, b):
    left, top = max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1])
    right, bottom = min(a[2], b[2]), min(a[3], b[3])
    intersection = ____
    area_a = max(0, a[2]-a[0]) * max(0, a[3]-a[1])
    area_b = max(0, b[2]-b[0]) * max(0, b[3]-b[1])
    union = ____
    return intersection / union if union else 0.0
challenge.solution:
def iou(a, b):
    left, top = max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1])
    right, bottom = min(a[2], b[2]), min(a[3], b[3])
    intersection = max(0, right-left) * max(0, bottom-top)
    area_a = max(0, a[2]-a[0]) * max(0, a[3]-a[1])
    area_b = max(0, b[2]-b[0]) * max(0, b[3]-b[1])
    union = area_a + area_b - intersection
    return intersection / union if union else 0.0
challenge.explanation: Clamping intersection dimensions handles separated boxes, and subtracting overlap prevents union from double-counting shared area.
hints: Multiply clamped intersection width and height.
Union adds both areas then subtracts intersection.
Guard a zero-area union.

lessons.title: Choose a Vision Model Family
lessons.summary: Match classification, detection, segmentation, and open-vocabulary capabilities to the product output.

contentBlocks.text: The output contract chooses the problem family

Classification labels an image, detection localizes instances with boxes, semantic segmentation labels pixels by class, and instance segmentation separates individual masks. Open-vocabulary models trade fixed-class optimization for flexible text-conditioned categories.
Selection constraints
A more detailed output requires more expensive labels and evaluation. Do not train masks when a coarse image-level decision is enough.

challenge.instructions: The product must outline and count each individual cracked panel. Choose the minimum suitable output family.

choices.text: Instance segmentation
Whole-image classification only
Text sentiment analysis

challenge.explanation: Individual masks provide both precise outlines and separate instance identities needed for counting overlapping panels.
hints: The output needs pixel boundaries.
It must distinguish multiple objects of the same class.

lessons.title: Suppress Duplicate Detections
lessons.summary: Implement greedy class-aware non-maximum suppression over scored boxes.

contentBlocks.text: One object can create many candidate boxes

Greedy NMS keeps the highest-scoring box, removes lower-scoring boxes of the same class whose IoU exceeds a threshold, and repeats. Class-aware suppression avoids deleting overlapping objects with different labels.

keep best
remaining = [d for d in remaining if d.class != best.class or iou(d,best) <= threshold]
Crowded scenes can contain distinct same-class objects with high overlap. Soft-NMS or learned post-processing may preserve recall better than hard deletion.

challenge.instructions: Sort by score, keep the best, and retain remaining detections of another class or IoU at most threshold.
challenge.starterCode:
def nms(detections, threshold, iou_fn):
    remaining = sorted(detections, key=lambda d: d["score"], reverse=True)
    kept = []
    while remaining:
        best = remaining.pop(0)
        kept.append(best)
        remaining = [candidate for candidate in remaining if ____]
    return kept
challenge.solution:
def nms(detections, threshold, iou_fn):
    remaining = sorted(detections, key=lambda d: d["score"], reverse=True)
    kept = []
    while remaining:
        best = remaining.pop(0)
        kept.append(best)
        remaining = [candidate for candidate in remaining if candidate["class"] != best["class"] or iou_fn(candidate["box"], best["box"]) <= threshold]
    return kept
challenge.explanation: Score order establishes priority, while the predicate suppresses only sufficiently overlapping candidates within the same class.
hints: Different classes always survive this comparison.
For the same class, keep when IoU is at most threshold.
Compare candidate box with best box.

modules.title: Serving Geometry and Evaluation
modules.summary: Map model outputs back to source coordinates, batch safely, deploy by constraint, and measure real slices.

lessons.title: Preprocessing and Postprocessing Are One Transform
lessons.summary: Carry invertible resize, pad, crop, and rotation metadata through the inference request.

contentBlocks.text: Predictions live in model coordinates

Letterboxing scales an image uniformly and adds padding. Model boxes must subtract that padding and divide by scale before display. Carry a transform object beside the tensor rather than reconstructing it from dimensions later.

source_x = (model_x - pad_x) / scale
source_y = (model_y - pad_y) / scale
Orientation metadata may mean stored pixel axes differ from visual axes. Normalize orientation before deriving the transform or include it explicitly in inversion.

challenge.instructions: Boxes are correct in model input but appear right and low on the original image. Identify a likely missing inversion.
challenge.explanation: The postprocessor likely failed to subtract letterbox padding before dividing by scale, leaving coordinates offset in both axes.
hints: The displacement is consistent across boxes.
Model input contained borders not present in source coordinates.
Invert operations in reverse order.

lessons.title: Invert Letterbox Coordinates
lessons.summary: Map a model-space box to clipped source-space coordinates.

contentBlocks.text: Undo padding before scaling
Letterbox forward order is scale then pad, so inversion subtracts pad then divides by scale. Clip output to source bounds because predicted boxes can extend into the padded border.
x1 = clamp((box.x1 - pad_x) / scale, 0, source_width)
Apply the identical floating-point convention in label generation, inference, and evaluation; off-by-one box edges can alter IoU near thresholds.

challenge.instructions: Subtract horizontal/vertical padding, divide by scale, and clamp x and y to source dimensions.
challenge.starterCode:
def invert_box(box, scale, pad_x, pad_y, width, height):
    x1 = (box[0] - pad_x) / scale
    y1 = (box[1] - pad_y) / scale
    x2 = (box[2] - pad_x) / scale
    y2 = (box[3] - pad_y) / scale
    return [____, ____, ____, ____]
challenge.solution:
def invert_box(box, scale, pad_x, pad_y, width, height):
    x1 = (box[0] - pad_x) / scale
    y1 = (box[1] - pad_y) / scale
    x2 = (box[2] - pad_x) / scale
    y2 = (box[3] - pad_y) / scale
    return [min(max(x1, 0), width), min(max(y1, 0), height), min(max(x2, 0), width), min(max(y2, 0), height)]

testCases.expected: coordinates clipped within width and height

challenge.explanation: Reverse-order arithmetic restores source units, and per-axis clamps prevent impossible display coordinates.
hints: Clamp x values between zero and width.
Clamp y values between zero and height.
Use min(max(value, 0), bound).

lessons.title: Batch Images without Mixing Transforms
lessons.summary: Group compatible tensor shapes while retaining per-image postprocessing metadata.

contentBlocks.text: Batching improves throughput but complicates identity

Dynamic batching collects requests for a short window and groups compatible model shapes. Every batch slot must retain request ID and transform; otherwise correct detections can be mapped onto the wrong source image.

batch_key = (model_version, input_height, input_width)
metadata[slot] = (request_id, transform)
Cap both wait time and batch size. Low traffic should not wait indefinitely for throughput that never arrives.

challenge.instructions: Group requests by model version and input shape while preserving original request objects in arrival order.

testCases.input: two same-shape requests and one different shape
testCases.expected: two buckets with original request order preserved

testCases.input: same shape but different model versions

challenge.explanation: The composite key prevents incompatible weights or dimensions from sharing a batch, while stored request objects retain identity and transforms.
hints: Initialize a list for unseen key.
Append request to buckets[key].
Model version is part of compatibility.

lessons.title: Choose Edge, Cloud, or Cascade
lessons.summary: Balance privacy, connectivity, model capacity, energy, and escalation quality.

contentBlocks.text: Deployment location changes the failure model

On-device vision offers privacy and immediate offline response but has memory and thermal limits. Cloud models can be larger and updated centrally but add transfer cost, latency, and data governance. A cascade handles easy cases locally and escalates uncertain cases under consent.
Cascade safeguards
Confidence alone may be miscalibrated under new cameras or lighting. Add out-of-distribution and input-quality signals before escalation decisions.

challenge.prompt: Inspect equipment in a disconnected facility
challenge.instructions: Images are sensitive, connectivity is intermittent, and rare uncertain cases may be reviewed later. Choose an architecture.

choices.text: Run a qualified local model, queue encrypted consented uncertain cases for later review, and retain an offline result path.
Require every frame to reach a cloud service synchronously.
Upload all camera footage indefinitely regardless of uncertainty.

challenge.explanation: Local inference satisfies privacy and availability, while bounded deferred escalation improves difficult cases without blocking operation.
hints: Connectivity cannot be on the critical path.
Most images need not leave the facility.
Uncertain cases can follow a controlled later workflow.

lessons.title: Evaluate Vision across Acquisition Conditions
lessons.summary: Break aggregate accuracy down by object size, camera, lighting, occlusion, and class.

contentBlocks.text: Image distributions fail in visible slices

Mean average precision summarizes detection across classes and IoU thresholds, but it can hide failure on tiny objects, night scenes, a new sensor, or rare safety classes. Evaluate the acquisition pipeline and postprocessing together.
Vision slices
items: Class and demographic context where appropriate

contentBlocks.text: Review false positives and false negatives as rendered overlays. Numeric summaries rarely reveal systematic coordinate or annotation defects.

challenge.instructions: A release keeps overall mAP but recall for small safety labels falls 20%. What should happen?

choices.text: Block or constrain rollout until the critical slice regression is understood and repaired.
Ship because the aggregate did not move.
Delete small-object labels from evaluation.

challenge.explanation: A high-impact slice can define product safety even when larger common objects keep the aggregate stable.
hints: Weight the consequence, not only frequency.
Aggregates can hide offsetting changes.

courses.title: Speech & Audio AI Systems
courses.summary: Engineer speech recognition, synthesis, diarization, and general audio classification from waveform preparation through serving and evaluation.

modules.title: Signal Preparation and Recognition
modules.summary: Turn sampled waveforms into calibrated features, segmented utterances, and timestamped recognition output.

lessons.title: Waveforms Become Time–Frequency Evidence
lessons.summary: Connect sample rate, windows, frequency bins, and log-mel features.

contentBlocks.text: Audio changes faster than one global spectrum can show

A sample rate records amplitude measurements per second and limits representable frequency below half that rate. Short-time Fourier analysis windows the waveform so a spectrogram preserves how energy across frequencies changes over time.
Feature contract
Resampling without an anti-alias filter can fold high-frequency energy into false lower frequencies that a model treats as real evidence.

challenge.instructions: Describe what happens when spectrogram hop size becomes smaller while window size stays fixed.
challenge.explanation: Frames overlap more, improving time sampling and increasing feature-frame count, compute, and storage; frequency resolution remains primarily tied to window length.
hints: Hop controls how far the window moves.
More overlap creates more frames.
Window length and hop have different roles.

lessons.title: Downmix without Clipping or Cancellation
lessons.summary: Handle stereo inputs and phase carefully before a mono speech model.

contentBlocks.text: Two channels are not safely combined by addition
Averaging channels controls level, but opposite-phase signals can cancel. Some recordings place different speakers on separate channels, making independent recognition preferable to downmixing.

mono = 0.5 * left + 0.5 * right
peak = max(abs(mono))
Inspect channel correlation, clipping, and content semantics before choosing a downmix rule.

challenge.instructions: Interviewer and guest were intentionally recorded on separate channels. What is the strongest starting point?

choices.text: Preserve channels and recognize each separately before aligning timestamps.
Discard one channel randomly.
Sum both channels at full gain regardless of clipping.

challenge.explanation: Separate channels already encode speaker separation, improving recognition and diarization while avoiding destructive mixing.
hints: The channel layout contains useful structure.
Downmixing would merge speakers unnecessarily.

lessons.title: Merge Overlapping ASR Windows
lessons.summary: Deduplicate timestamped words produced by overlapping recognition segments.

contentBlocks.text: Overlap preserves boundary words and creates duplicates

Long audio is decoded in overlapping windows to avoid cutting phonemes. Merge words in time order and reject a candidate when its normalized text matches the previous word and their time intervals overlap.

overlap = candidate.start < previous.end
same = normalize(candidate.text) == normalize(previous.text)
Real alignment may require sequence matching across several words; timestamp-only deduplication can remove legitimate repeated speech.

challenge.instructions: Sort words by start and skip only same normalized text that begins before the previous kept word ends.

testCases.expected: both retained because speech repeats without overlap

challenge.explanation: Time overlap distinguishes window duplication from an intentional repeated word occurring later.
hints: Compare candidate start with previous end.
Use strict less-than for overlap.
Append whenever the duplicate condition is false.

lessons.title: Choose Streaming or Batch Recognition
lessons.summary: Match recognition architecture to latency, revision, context, and throughput requirements.

contentBlocks.text: Future audio improves accuracy but delays output

Streaming ASR emits low-latency partial hypotheses using limited future context. Batch ASR can use the full utterance and often improves punctuation, segmentation, and long-range disambiguation. Hybrid systems stream interaction text then finalize asynchronously.
Decision criteria
Downstream actions should wait for a stable or final hypothesis when a recognition revision could change intent.

challenge.instructions: Clinicians need immediate text but final records require high accuracy. Choose a pipeline.

choices.text: Stream clearly marked partials, then replace with a higher-context final transcript before record commitment.
Treat every first partial as immutable clinical truth.
Wait hours before showing any feedback.

challenge.explanation: The two-stage design supports interaction while reserving authoritative storage for a finalized, validated transcript.
hints: Immediate display and final accuracy are separate requirements.
Mark revisable content honestly.
Commit only after finalization.

lessons.title: Calibrate Recognition Confidence
lessons.summary: Bin predictions to compare stated confidence with observed word correctness.

contentBlocks.text: A score becomes useful when it predicts error frequency

Raw decoder probability is often overconfident and length-dependent. Calibration compares confidence buckets with empirical correctness on representative noise, language, and device slices, then supports review or clarification thresholds.

bin_accuracy = correct_count / count
bin_confidence = sum(confidence) / count
Calibration can drift when microphones or languages change even if overall word error rate remains similar.

challenge.instructions: For each bin, return count, average confidence, and correctness rate.
challenge.starterCode:
def summarize_bins(items, bin_count):
    bins = [{"count":0, "confidence":0.0, "correct":0} for _ in range(bin_count)]
    for item in items:
        index = min(int(item["confidence"] * bin_count), bin_count - 1)
        bucket = bins[index]
        bucket["count"] += 1
        bucket["confidence"] += item["confidence"]
        bucket["correct"] += int(item["correct"])
    return [{"count": b["count"], "avg_confidence": ____, "accuracy": ____} for b in bins if b["count"]]
challenge.solution:
def summarize_bins(items, bin_count):
    bins = [{"count":0, "confidence":0.0, "correct":0} for _ in range(bin_count)]
    for item in items:
        index = min(int(item["confidence"] * bin_count), bin_count - 1)
        bucket = bins[index]
        bucket["count"] += 1
        bucket["confidence"] += item["confidence"]
        bucket["correct"] += int(item["correct"])
    return [{"count": b["count"], "avg_confidence": b["confidence"] / b["count"], "accuracy": b["correct"] / b["count"]} for b in bins if b["count"]]

testCases.input: two items confidence .8 and 1.0, one correct
testCases.expected: bin averages and accuracy derived from its own count

challenge.explanation: Each nonempty bucket normalizes summed confidence and correct outcomes by the same observed count.
hints: Average confidence is its sum divided by count.
Accuracy is correct divided by count.
Empty buckets are already filtered.

modules.title: Speakers, Synthesis, and Evaluation
modules.summary: Separate speakers, synthesize safely, and evaluate intelligibility and identity across real conditions.

lessons.title: Diarization Answers Who Spoke When
lessons.summary: Connect speech segmentation, speaker embeddings, clustering, and overlap detection.

contentBlocks.text: Transcription and speaker assignment are separate

Diarization segments speech, represents segments with speaker embeddings, and clusters similar voices. Alignment then assigns recognized words to speaker intervals; overlapping speech may require multiple simultaneous labels.
Common errors
items: One speaker split into several clusters
Overlapping speech assigned to one person
Known identity confused with anonymous cluster

contentBlocks.text: Speaker recognition identifies a known person and raises biometric concerns; diarization can keep anonymous labels such as Speaker 1.

challenge.instructions: Two people talk at once, but the output format allows one speaker per timestamp. Describe the representational failure.
challenge.explanation: The schema cannot express overlapping speakers, so one voice must be dropped or time-assigned incorrectly; the output contract needs multi-label overlap intervals.
hints: The world has two active sources.
The current schema permits one.
Model capability cannot fix an insufficient representation.

lessons.title: Interpret Diarization Error
lessons.summary: Separate missed speech, false alarm speech, and speaker confusion.

contentBlocks.text: Diarization can fail in three different ways

Missed speech labels real speech as silence, false alarm labels nonspeech as speech, and confusion assigns speech to the wrong speaker. Diarization error rate aggregates their durations but component rates point to different repairs.
DER = (miss + false_alarm + confusion) / reference_speech_time
Scoring often uses a boundary collar and explicit overlap policy; report them so DER comparisons remain meaningful.

challenge.instructions: All speech regions are detected, but many segments are attributed to the other participant. Which component dominates?

choices.text: Speaker confusion
Missed speech
False alarm speech

challenge.explanation: Speech timing is present, but identity assignment is wrong, which contributes confusion duration.
hints: No speech was lost.
The error concerns who, not whether, someone spoke.

lessons.title: Crossfade Synthesized Audio Chunks
lessons.summary: Blend adjacent waveform chunks to reduce clicks at streaming synthesis boundaries.

contentBlocks.text: Waveform discontinuities sound like clicks

Independent TTS chunks can begin at a different amplitude or phase than the previous chunk ends. A short crossfade linearly decreases the old tail while increasing the new head, then appends the remaining audio.
mixed[i] = old_tail[i] * (1-alpha) + new_head[i] * alpha
Crossfading cannot repair mismatched voice, prosody, or sample rate. Preserve synthesis state and normalize format before stitching.

challenge.instructions: Blend overlap samples with alpha rising from 0 to 1, then append the non-overlapping new tail.
challenge.starterCode:
def crossfade(previous, new, overlap):
    overlap = min(overlap, len(previous), len(new))
    prefix = previous[:-overlap] if overlap else previous[:]
    mixed = []
    for index in range(overlap):
        alpha = (index + 1) / (overlap + 1)
        mixed.append(____)
    return prefix + mixed + ____
challenge.solution:
def crossfade(previous, new, overlap):
    overlap = min(overlap, len(previous), len(new))
    prefix = previous[:-overlap] if overlap else previous[:]
    mixed = []
    for index in range(overlap):
        alpha = (index + 1) / (overlap + 1)
        mixed.append(previous[len(previous)-overlap+index] * (1-alpha) + new[index] * alpha)
    return prefix + mixed + new[overlap:]

testCases.expected: one blended boundary sample then remaining new tail
previous followed by all new samples

challenge.explanation: Complementary weights blend the two boundary signals, and slicing avoids duplicating the new samples consumed by overlap.
hints: Index the final overlap samples of previous.
Weight previous by 1-alpha and new by alpha.
Append new[overlap:] afterward.

lessons.title: Govern Voice Identity and Consent
lessons.summary: Constrain speaker adaptation with authorization, provenance, disclosure, and revocation.

contentBlocks.text: A synthetic voice can impersonate a person

Voice cloning needs explicit subject consent, authorized use scope, secure reference audio, output disclosure, and a revocation path. High-risk voices and public figures may require prohibition rather than a softer prompt rule.
Control points
A checkbox from the requester does not prove the recorded speaker consented. Bind consent to the subject identity and source audio.

challenge.instructions: Choose the strongest operational design.

choices.text: Use a contracted voice actor with scoped consent, signed profile, disclosed synthetic output, audit logs, and revocation.
Clone any employee from a meeting recording without asking.
Let prompt text decide whether impersonation is acceptable.

challenge.explanation: It establishes provenance, consent, bounded use, user transparency, and operational control over the identity asset.
hints: Consent must come from the voice subject.
The permission needs scope and lifetime.
Plan for abuse and withdrawal.

lessons.title: Evaluate Meaning, Timing, and Perception
lessons.summary: Combine task metrics with human listening and slice tests for speech and sound systems.

contentBlocks.text: No single audio metric captures usefulness

Word error rate measures edit distance but weights all word edits similarly. Keyword recall, semantic accuracy, timestamp error, speaker attribution, intelligibility, naturalness, and robustness under noise answer different product questions.
Evaluation slices
Human listening studies should randomize order and level-match samples; otherwise loudness and presentation bias can dominate preference.

challenge.instructions: Which metric deserves priority beyond overall word error rate?

choices.text: Recall and false-trigger rate for the critical command phrases by noise slice.
Average transcript character count.
TTS voice popularity only.

challenge.explanation: The product risk depends on missing or spuriously triggering specific commands, particularly under difficult acoustic conditions.
hints: Not every word has equal consequence.
Measure both misses and accidental activations.

courses.title: Search, Ranking & Recommenders
courses.summary: Engineer candidate generation, learned ranking, feedback-aware recommendations, exploration, and online experiments without amplifying bias blindly.

modules.title: Candidate and Ranking Funnels
modules.summary: Retrieve broadly, score with richer features, and preserve online/offline feature consistency.

lessons.title: Ranking Optimizes an Ordered Experience
lessons.summary: Separate candidate recall, position-aware ranking, and product utility.

contentBlocks.text: A list has scarce attention at the top

Search and recommendation first generate plausible candidates, then rank them using query, user, item, and context signals. The objective should reflect useful outcomes, not merely clicks that position and presentation strongly influence.
Funnel measurements
A ranker cannot promote an item absent from candidate generation. Evaluate every stage against its own responsibility.

challenge.instructions: The relevant item never enters the 100 candidates. What can the reranker do?
challenge.explanation: Nothing: it can only reorder supplied candidates, so candidate-source coverage or retrieval recall must change first.
hints: List the reranker’s input set.
Later stages cannot recover missing items.
Locate the earliest failing stage.

lessons.title: Choose Position-Aware Metrics
lessons.summary: Distinguish precision@k, reciprocal rank, and normalized discounted cumulative gain.

contentBlocks.text: Different metrics reward different list behavior

Precision@k counts relevant items in the visible set. Reciprocal rank emphasizes the first relevant result. NDCG supports graded relevance and discounts useful items appearing lower, normalized by the ideal ordering.
DCG@k = Σ gain(relevance_i) / log2(i + 1)
Offline relevance labels often reflect old ranking exposure. Metric precision cannot remove collection bias from the labels themselves.

challenge.instructions: Users usually need the first correct destination. Which metric directly emphasizes how early that first relevant result appears?

choices.text: Mean reciprocal rank
Training row count
Average item title length

challenge.explanation: Reciprocal rank gives 1/rank of the first relevant result, directly rewarding earlier first success.
hints: Only the first correct destination matters strongly.
The metric should change with its position.

lessons.title: Compute Discounted Cumulative Gain
lessons.summary: Implement graded gain with logarithmic position discount.

contentBlocks.text: High relevance matters most near the top
A common gain is 2^relevance − 1, which distinguishes highly relevant results sharply. Dividing by log2(position + 1), with positions starting at one, reduces credit lower in the list.

gain = (2 ** relevance) - 1
discount = log2(position + 1)
