NDCG divides DCG by the ideal DCG for the same labels; define the zero-ideal case to return zero.

challenge.instructions: Sum exponential gain divided by log2(position + 1) for the first k relevance labels.
challenge.starterCode:
from math import log2

def dcg(relevances, k):
    total = 0.0
    for position, relevance in enumerate(relevances[:k], start=1):
        gain = ____
        discount = ____
        total += gain / discount
    return total
challenge.solution:
from math import log2

def dcg(relevances, k):
    total = 0.0
    for position, relevance in enumerate(relevances[:k], start=1):
        gain = (2 ** relevance) - 1
        discount = log2(position + 1)
        total += gain / discount
    return total
challenge.explanation: Exponential gain rewards stronger grades, and logarithmic discount decreases their contribution with rank.
hints: Gain is two to relevance minus one.
Discount uses log2(position + 1).
Slice inputs to k before enumerating.

lessons.title: Design a Two-Stage Ranker
lessons.summary: Allocate cheap features to broad retrieval and expensive interactions to a bounded candidate set.

contentBlocks.text: Spend model capacity where it changes the visible list

Candidate generation may combine lexical, embedding, collaborative, and rule-based sources. A lightweight ranker narrows thousands to hundreds; a richer model scores cross-features for the final page under a latency deadline.
Production safeguards
Apply hard legal and inventory eligibility before personalized ranking so the model never learns to trade compliance against engagement.

challenge.prompt: Rank a catalog of ten million items
challenge.instructions: Choose a latency-conscious architecture that still uses expensive user-item interaction features.

choices.text: Retrieve a high-recall candidate pool cheaply, then apply the expensive ranker only to that bounded set.
Run the largest cross-encoder over all ten million items per request.
Ignore eligibility until after rendering.

challenge.explanation: The funnel reserves costly pairwise scoring for plausible candidates while maintaining an explicit candidate-recall target.
hints: The full catalog is too large for rich scoring.
Cheap retrieval must protect recall.
Filter ineligible inventory early.

lessons.title: Join Features as of Request Time
lessons.summary: Select the latest feature event not later than the ranking timestamp.

contentBlocks.text: Future features create ranking leakage

Offline examples must reconstruct values known at the original request time. An as-of join chooses the newest event whose timestamp is less than or equal to the request timestamp, matching online feature semantics.

eligible = [e for e in events if e.time <= request_time]
feature = max(eligible, key=lambda e: e.time)
Store feature definition version and event availability time, not only event occurrence time; late-arriving data was not actually available online.

challenge.instructions: Return the value from the latest event at or before the request time, or the default when none qualifies.
challenge.explanation: Filtering by availability prevents future information, and maximum qualifying time reproduces the freshest value the online system could have seen.
hints: Compare available_at with request_time.
Choose max by available_at.
Return default for an empty eligible set.

modules.title: Feedback, Exploration, and Experiments
modules.summary: Learn cautiously from biased interactions and measure long-term effects through controlled exposure.

lessons.title: Recommendations Change Their Own Data
lessons.summary: Recognize exposure, position, popularity, and selection bias in interaction logs.

contentBlocks.text: Observed clicks are outcomes of the previous policy

Users can click only items they see, and top positions attract attention independent of relevance. Training directly on clicks reinforces past exposure and can create popularity loops that starve new or niche items of evidence.
Log the decision context
Negative feedback is ambiguous when an item was never shown. Missing interaction is not automatically a negative label.

challenge.instructions: Describe how ranking by clicks alone can make already popular items increasingly dominant.
challenge.explanation: Popular items receive higher rank and more impressions, generating more clicks partly from exposure; retraining treats those clicks as relevance and increases their future exposure again.
hints: Clicks require impressions.
Rank influences observation.
The next model trains on outcomes of the prior model.

lessons.title: Interpret Implicit Feedback Carefully
lessons.summary: Distinguish clicks, dwell, skips, purchases, and satisfaction as noisy signals.

contentBlocks.text: An action is not a pure relevance label

A click may reflect curiosity or a misleading title. Long dwell can mean engagement or confusion. Purchases are sparse and affected by price. Combine signals, define attribution windows, and validate them against explicit satisfaction outcomes.
Label design checks
items: Can bots or accidental actions contaminate it?

contentBlocks.text: Train and evaluate with the same outcome horizon; a seven-day purchase label cannot be complete one hour after impression.

challenge.instructions: A candidate was eligible but never displayed. How should its lack of click be interpreted?

choices.text: As unobserved, not a confident negative interaction.
As proof the user hated it.
As a completed purchase.

challenge.explanation: Without exposure the user had no opportunity to act, so the counterfactual preference is unknown.
hints: Interaction requires visibility.
Separate eligible, shown, and clicked states.

lessons.title: Greedily Rerank for Diversity
lessons.summary: Trade relevance against redundancy using maximal marginal relevance.

contentBlocks.text: Ten near-duplicates waste a ten-slot page

Maximal marginal relevance selects an item by relevance minus a redundancy penalty against already selected items. Lambda controls the balance: one favors original relevance only; lower values increase diversity pressure.
score = lambda_ * relevance - (1-lambda_) * max_similarity_to_selected
Diversity needs a meaningful similarity representation and should not override hard relevance or safety thresholds.

challenge.instructions: Return the candidate with highest lambda-weighted relevance minus redundancy to selected items.

testCases.expected: candidate with highest relevance regardless of similarity

challenge.explanation: The nested score explicitly penalizes similarity only when prior items exist, and max selects the strongest trade-off.
hints: Multiply relevance by lambda_.
Subtract one-minus-lambda times redundancy.
Pass the mmr function as max key.

lessons.title: Explore without Sacrificing Guardrails
lessons.summary: Collect counterfactual evidence through bounded randomized exposure.

contentBlocks.text: A deterministic policy cannot learn about unseen choices

Exploration assigns some eligible traffic to alternatives so the system learns their outcomes. Restrict exploration to safe candidates, cap utility loss, log selection probabilities, and protect vulnerable or high-stakes contexts.
Exploration controls
Randomization probability must be logged for unbiased off-policy estimation; otherwise observed outcomes cannot be corrected for selection.

challenge.instructions: Choose a responsible strategy for testing new lessons in recommendations.

choices.text: Randomize a small eligible slice above a quality floor, log propensity, monitor learning outcomes, and cap repeat exposure.
Show unreviewed content to every learner at the top position.
Never expose any new item, then infer its quality from no data.

challenge.explanation: Bounded exploration creates evidence while preserving quality constraints, auditability, and rapid intervention.
hints: Learning requires some exposure.
Exposure should remain eligible and measurable.
Log how each item was selected.

lessons.title: Interpret an Online Ranking Experiment
lessons.summary: Read primary, guardrail, novelty, and long-term metrics before rollout.

contentBlocks.text: A click lift can hide worse recommendations

Online tests need a predeclared primary outcome and guardrails such as dissatisfaction, latency, diversity, creator concentration, and delayed retention. Novelty effects and interference can invalidate a short naive comparison.
Experiment discipline
Stopping when a metric first becomes significant inflates false-positive risk; use the planned horizon or valid sequential methods.

challenge.instructions: Clicks rise 4%, but completed learning sessions fall 6% and complaints rise. What is the sound decision?

choices.text: Do not roll out broadly; the proxy improved while core outcome and guardrail regressed.
Ship because click-through rate is always the true objective.
Remove complaint logging from the dashboard.

challenge.explanation: Clicks are a proxy, while completed sessions and complaints indicate degraded learner value and trust.
hints: Identify the actual product outcome.
Guardrails can veto a proxy lift.

courses.title: Synthetic Data & Data Engines
courses.summary: Generate targeted training and evaluation data with provenance, validators, deduplication, privacy controls, and feedback loops tied to real failures.

modules.title: Controlled Generation and Quality
modules.summary: Choose where synthetic examples help, preserve provenance, and filter them through independent checks.

lessons.title: Synthetic Data Needs a Named Purpose
lessons.summary: Use generation for coverage, formatting, simulation, or privacy—not as a vague replacement for reality.

contentBlocks.text: Generated examples inherit a generator’s blind spots

Synthetic data can cover rare combinations, expand instruction formats, simulate controlled environments, and create adversarial cases. It cannot establish the true frequency or causal structure of a population unless the simulator already models those properties accurately.
Attach to every example
Keep synthetic and observed examples distinguishable through training and evaluation so their effects can be measured rather than silently blended.

challenge.instructions: Explain why synthetic examples can test a parser’s date formats but cannot by themselves estimate how often each format occurs among customers.
challenge.explanation: Generation can deliberately enumerate format cases, but its sampling distribution reflects prompts and generator behavior rather than the real customer population frequency.
hints: Separate coverage from prevalence.
Who determines how often each example is generated?
Real frequency requires observed sampling evidence.

lessons.title: Prevent Evaluation Contamination
lessons.summary: Keep held-out targets and their near-duplicates out of generation and training paths.

contentBlocks.text: A generated paraphrase can still leak the answer

If evaluation examples appear in a generator prompt, retrieval context, or seed pool, synthetic outputs may copy their structure or labels. Split sources before generation and scan semantic as well as exact duplicates across all datasets.

source_pool = training_sources_only
assert nearest_similarity(candidate, heldout_index) < threshold
Using a held-out failure to design a specific training example is targeted iteration, but that case no longer supports an unbiased final estimate; maintain a fresh test set.

challenge.instructions: Which workflow best preserves an untouched final test?

choices.text: Generate from training sources only, deduplicate against held-out data, and lock final-test access.
Include final answers in every generation prompt.
Train until final-test score stops improving.

challenge.explanation: It separates source influence, detects near-copy leakage, and prevents repeated adaptation to final-test cases.
hints: Generation is part of the training pipeline.
Near-duplicates matter, not only exact strings.

lessons.title: Build a Layered Example Validator
lessons.summary: Collect schema, invariant, and provenance errors before accepting generated records.

contentBlocks.text: Generator output is untrusted input

Validation starts with parse and schema, then domain invariants, reference consistency, safety policy, duplication, and optional independent grading. Preserve error codes and rejected artifacts for quality analysis rather than silently regenerating forever.

errors = schema_errors(record) + domain_errors(record)
if errors: quarantine(record, errors)
A validator produced by the same prompt and model may share the generator’s failure mode. Use deterministic checks and independent evidence wherever possible.

challenge.instructions: Collect errors for blank input, unsupported label, or missing generator version.

testCases.input: blank input, invalid label, no version

challenge.explanation: Independent checks accumulate all defects, giving the data pipeline actionable diagnostics instead of one opaque pass/fail bit.
hints: Append unsupported_label for a label outside the allowlist.
Append missing_provenance when version is absent.
Do not return early after one error.

lessons.title: Design a Reproducible Generation Pipeline
lessons.summary: Separate planning, generation, deterministic checks, independent review, and publishing.

contentBlocks.text: Generation is one stage in a governed build

A coverage planner defines target cells and quotas. Workers generate candidate artifacts with seeds and lineage. Validators filter, reviewers sample by risk, and a publisher creates an immutable dataset manifest with aggregate quality reports.
Failure controls
Unlimited regenerate-until-pass loops select for validator exploitation and hide how hard a target is. Track attempt count and stop explicitly.

challenge.instructions: Choose a pipeline that makes quality and selection bias visible.

choices.text: Define target taxonomy, cap attempts, record every candidate and rejection, use deterministic plus independent review, and publish a manifest.
Regenerate silently until one judge says pass.
Discard provenance after merging examples.

challenge.explanation: The governed pipeline reveals generation difficulty, validator behavior, coverage, and lineage while preventing unbounded selection pressure.
hints: Rejected examples are quality evidence.
The number of attempts changes selection.
Publishing needs reproducible identity.

lessons.title: Allocate Deterministic Generation Seeds
lessons.summary: Derive stable per-cell seeds so retries and distributed workers reproduce the same plan.

contentBlocks.text: Reproducibility begins before sampling

A global seed alone can change downstream examples when task ordering changes. Derive each seed from dataset version, target-cell ID, and example index with a stable hash so workers can resume independently.

material = f"{version}|{cell}|{index}"
seed = stable_hash(material)
Seed reproduction still depends on model, runtime, and decoding implementation versions; record all of them in lineage.

challenge.instructions: Return deterministic integer seeds from SHA-256 of version, cell, and index separated by pipes.
challenge.starterCode:
import hashlib

def seed_for(version, cell, index):
    material = ____
    digest = hashlib.sha256(material.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
    return ____
challenge.explanation: Canonical material makes identity unambiguous, and a stable cryptographic digest avoids process-randomized language hash behavior.
hints: Join the three fields with literal pipe separators.
Convert a fixed digest prefix from base 16.
Do not use Python's randomized hash().

modules.title: Data Engines, Privacy, and Evaluation
modules.summary: Turn observed failures into prioritized data work while controlling judge bias, duplicates, and memorization risk.

lessons.title: A Data Engine Converts Failures into Coverage
lessons.summary: Close the loop from production evidence through taxonomy, curation, training, and fresh evaluation.

contentBlocks.text: The flywheel needs a steering signal

Collect consented failures and uncertainty signals, cluster them into a taxonomy, estimate impact and coverage gaps, then choose whether to relabel real data, synthesize controlled variants, change evaluation, or repair the system without retraining.
Prioritize a failure cluster by
Do not train immediately on every complaint. First determine whether the cause is data, prompt, retrieval, policy, interface, or instrumentation.

challenge.instructions: Retrieved evidence is correct, but links point to wrong URLs due to metadata mapping. Should the first response be synthetic training data?
challenge.explanation: No. The defect is deterministic citation metadata mapping, so repair and test that component rather than asking model training to compensate.
hints: Locate the first failing component.
The model had correct evidence.
Prefer a direct deterministic repair.

lessons.title: Audit Automated Data Judges
lessons.summary: Detect position, verbosity, self-preference, and rubric interpretation bias.

contentBlocks.text: A judge model is another measurement instrument

Automated judges can prefer longer answers, certain phrasing, or outputs from related model families. Calibrate against blinded expert labels, randomize candidate order, test swapped positions, and report agreement by slice.
Judge controls
High judge-model consistency can mean stable bias. Agreement with itself is not validity.

challenge.instructions: Which experiment directly tests whether the judge favors the first answer?

choices.text: Evaluate identical pairs in both A/B orders and compare preference reversals.
Always put the preferred system first.
Increase judge temperature without measurement.

challenge.explanation: Swapping positions holds content constant while changing only order, isolating position preference.
hints: Control every factor except position.
A valid preference should follow content after swapping.

lessons.title: Filter Near-Duplicates by Similarity
lessons.summary: Keep the first representative and reject later candidates above a similarity threshold.

contentBlocks.text: Duplicates distort both learning and evaluation

Exact hashes catch byte copies but miss paraphrases and templated variants. A streaming filter compares each candidate with accepted representatives, stores the maximum similarity and source pair, and rejects above a tuned threshold.

if max(similarity(candidate, kept) for kept in accepted) >= threshold:
    reject(candidate)
Overaggressive semantic deduplication can erase legitimate hard cases that share topic but differ in the decisive constraint. Review threshold-near pairs.

challenge.instructions: Accept the first item and later items only when every accepted similarity is below threshold.

testCases.input: first item then identical item with threshold .9

challenge.explanation: The default accepts the first item, and strict below-threshold comparison preserves only sufficiently distinct later examples.
hints: Accept when maximum is less than threshold.
Append item to accepted.
Preserve input order for deterministic representatives.

lessons.title: Limit Memorization and Reidentification
lessons.summary: Treat synthetic output as potentially derived from private sources, not automatically anonymous.

contentBlocks.text: Synthetic does not guarantee private

A generator trained or conditioned on sensitive records may reproduce rare strings or preserve identifying combinations. Minimize source data, strip direct identifiers, constrain prompts, scan outputs, measure membership or extraction risk, and apply formal privacy methods when required.
Release review
Differential privacy provides a quantified training guarantee only under a correctly accounted mechanism; it is not a label to apply after ordinary generation.

challenge.instructions: Tickets contain names, order IDs, and rare personal situations. Choose the safer architecture.

choices.text: Minimize and redact sources, generate under bounded templates, scan against source similarity and identifiers, then human-review high-risk slices.
Prompt with raw tickets and publish all outputs because they are called synthetic.
Remove only the name field while preserving unique account numbers.

challenge.explanation: Layered minimization, controlled generation, output comparison, and risk-based review address both direct copying and reidentifying combinations.
hints: Rare combinations can identify without a name.
Inspect outputs against their sources.
Synthetic origin does not erase provenance.

lessons.title: Measure the Synthetic Mixture, Not Just Volume
lessons.summary: Run controlled ablations by source, slice, and mixture weight on untouched real evaluation data.

contentBlocks.text: More generated rows can reduce real performance

Compare a real-only baseline with several synthetic mixture weights under identical training budgets. Evaluate on untouched observed cases, inspect target slices and regressions, and track whether gains come from diversity rather than simple repetition.
Mixture experiment
Training longer because the synthetic dataset is larger confounds data composition with compute. Match update budgets or report both effects.

challenge.instructions: A model improves only on a synthetic validation set created by the same generator, while real holdout performance falls. What does this show?

choices.text: Likely generator-distribution overfitting, not a demonstrated real-world gain.
The real holdout should be discarded.
Synthetic volume guarantees better deployment performance.

challenge.explanation: Shared generator artifacts can make train and validation look aligned while transfer to observed data deteriorates.
hints: Ask whether evaluation is independent of generation.
Deployment resembles observed data more than the generator’s style.

courses.title: Reasoning, Planning & Test-Time Compute
courses.summary: Allocate inference effort adaptively, aggregate diverse candidates, verify intermediate work, and execute plans through bounded state transitions.

modules.title: Spend Inference Compute Deliberately
modules.summary: Decide when more samples, deeper search, or stronger verification actually improve expected utility.

lessons.title: Test-Time Compute Is a Search Budget
lessons.summary: Understand sampling, branching, revision, and verification as ways to explore candidate solutions.

contentBlocks.text: More inference can improve hard tasks—and waste easy ones

Test-time scaling spends additional tokens or model calls to generate alternatives, critique them, search states, or apply verifiers. Gains depend on candidate diversity and a selection signal correlated with true correctness.
Compute strategies
If every sample repeats the same misconception or the verifier rewards fluent errors, more compute concentrates failure rather than correcting it.

challenge.instructions: Why might increasing candidates from 1 to 8 help more than increasing from 64 to 71?
challenge.explanation: Early samples can add meaningful solution diversity, while later samples increasingly duplicate existing paths and add selection cost; marginal success probability usually falls.
hints: Consider duplicate candidate probability.
Selection becomes harder as weak candidates accumulate.
Measure marginal gain per added token.

lessons.title: Route Easy and Hard Requests Differently
lessons.summary: Use calibrated difficulty signals instead of applying maximum reasoning to every request.

contentBlocks.text: Adaptive inference protects latency and cost

A router may use task type, input complexity, initial uncertainty, verifier disagreement, or a lightweight difficulty model. Thresholds should be calibrated on outcomes and constrained by user deadline and impact.
Low confidence can reflect unfamiliar formatting rather than true difficulty. Evaluate routing false positives and false negatives by slice.

challenge.instructions: The task is 17 + 25, a calculator tool is available, and latency matters. Choose the best route.

choices.text: Use the deterministic calculator with a minimal response budget.
Generate 100 long reasoning traces and vote.
Sample until two minutes expire.

challenge.explanation: Exact arithmetic has a cheap reliable tool, so additional generative search adds cost without expected utility.
hints: Use deterministic computation for exact arithmetic.
Difficulty and impact are both low.

lessons.title: Aggregate Normalized Candidate Answers
lessons.summary: Count equivalent final answers and break ties by summed verifier confidence.

contentBlocks.text: Voting requires an equivalence rule

Candidates may express the same answer with formatting differences. Normalize only what the task permits, group by the normalized result, then compare vote count and independent verification evidence—not reasoning length.

groups[normalize(answer)].append(candidate)
key = max(groups, key=lambda g: (len(groups[g]), sum(score)))
Majority voting assumes error diversity. Correlated samples from one prompt and model can agree confidently on the same mistake.

challenge.instructions: Group candidates by stripped lowercase answer; choose highest count, then highest summed verifier score.

testCases.input: two tied answer groups with score sums .8 and 1.4

challenge.explanation: Normalization unifies superficial variants, vote count remains primary, and verifier evidence resolves equal support.
hints: First tuple component is len(groups[key]).
Second sums verifier_score in the group.
Return None for no candidates.

lessons.title: Separate Proposer and Verifier Roles
lessons.summary: Use executable checks, constraints, or independently trained scorers to select candidate solutions.

contentBlocks.text: Generation and checking have different information needs

A proposer explores possible solutions; a verifier tests them against unit tests, constraints, retrieved evidence, simulators, or a rubric. Keep hidden tests and authoritative state outside proposer context when gaming is possible.
Verifier hierarchy
Verifier optimization creates pressure to exploit its blind spots. Maintain adversarial holdouts and periodically inspect high-scoring failures.

challenge.instructions: Choose the strongest candidate-selection architecture for a sandboxed programming task.

choices.text: Run candidates against hidden unit and resource tests, then rank passing solutions by explicit criteria.
Choose the longest explanation without executing code.
Ask each candidate whether it is correct and trust yes.

challenge.explanation: Executable hidden checks provide task-grounded evidence and reduce reward hacking compared with stylistic or self-reported signals.
hints: Correctness is executable here.
Keep some tests outside the proposer context.
Validate resource behavior as well as outputs.

lessons.title: Allocate Compute by Marginal Value
lessons.summary: Grant one additional step at a time to the unresolved task with highest expected gain per unit cost.

contentBlocks.text: Budget allocation is a scheduling problem

Each task estimates the expected quality gain and cost of its next inference step. A greedy scheduler selects the highest positive gain-per-cost option that fits the remaining budget, then updates estimates after observing the result.

utility = expected_gain / cost
choose max utility among steps with cost <= remaining
Gain estimates must be calibrated and uncertainty-aware; systematically underestimated groups may otherwise receive less compute and worse service.

challenge.instructions: Among unfinished options that fit budget and have positive gain, return the one with highest gain/cost or None.
challenge.explanation: Filtering enforces feasibility and positive value, while the ratio compares expected marginal improvement per budget unit.
hints: Divide expected_gain by cost.
The eligibility filter already removes finished tasks.
Return None when no step fits.

modules.title: Planning, Execution, and Evaluation
modules.summary: Represent state and dependencies explicitly, replan on evidence, and test long-horizon behavior under perturbation.

lessons.title: Plans Connect States through Actions
lessons.summary: Define preconditions, effects, observations, and goals before asking for a sequence.

contentBlocks.text: A plan is only valid relative to a state model

An action has preconditions that must hold and effects that update state. Execution produces observations that may differ from expected effects. A goal predicate and cost function define when to stop and which valid plans are preferable.
Planning contract
Natural-language plans are proposals. The executor must recheck preconditions against current authoritative state before every effect.

challenge.prompt: Explain why a valid plan can become invalid
challenge.instructions: Inventory changes after planning but before execution. What should the executor do?
challenge.explanation: Re-read authoritative inventory, reject the stale action whose precondition no longer holds, update state, and replan or request guidance within the remaining budget.
hints: Plans use a snapshot.
External state can change concurrently.
Preconditions are checked at execution time.

lessons.title: Replan on Material State Change
lessons.summary: Distinguish recoverable action retries from evidence that invalidates the remaining plan.

contentBlocks.text: Not every failure deserves the same response

A transient timeout with idempotent action may be retried. A failed precondition, changed goal, newly discovered dependency, or exhausted resource changes the planning state and requires revising downstream steps.
Bound replanning cycles. A system that oscillates between two invalid plans needs escalation, not infinite reflection.

challenge.instructions: Step 2 requires a dataset that was deleted after the plan was created. What is the correct response?

choices.text: Update state and replan remaining steps because a precondition is permanently false.
Retry the same call forever.
Pretend step 2 succeeded.

challenge.explanation: The world state changed materially, so repetition cannot restore the missing resource and downstream dependencies must be reconsidered.
hints: Classify transient versus persistent failure.
The remaining plan assumed the resource existed.

lessons.title: Validate a Plan Dependency Graph
lessons.summary: Reject missing dependencies and cycles before scheduling plan steps.

contentBlocks.text: A dependency cycle can never become ready
Represent steps by stable IDs and dependency IDs. Validate references, then use Kahn’s algorithm: start with zero-indegree steps, remove their outgoing edges, and require every step to be visited.

ready = [step for step in steps if indegree[step] == 0]
valid = visited_count == len(steps)
Graph validity does not prove action preconditions or permissions; it only establishes a schedulable dependency order.

challenge.instructions: Return false for unknown dependency IDs; otherwise topologically visit and require all steps.

testCases.input: a depends on b and b depends on a
a then b depends on a

challenge.explanation: Only dependency-free steps enter the ready set; a cycle leaves nodes unvisited, while unknown references fail before traversal.
hints: Append a step when its dependency set becomes empty.
Compare visited with number of steps.
Cycles never reach zero indegree.

lessons.title: Execute Plans inside Capability Sandboxes
lessons.summary: Constrain filesystem, network, credentials, time, and side effects per action.

contentBlocks.text: Planning scope must not expand execution authority

Each plan step receives only the tool capabilities, paths, domains, secrets, and resource limits it requires. Consequential actions pass policy and approval gates; intermediate outputs become immutable artifacts with provenance.
Sandbox boundaries
A correct high-level goal does not authorize arbitrary means. Policy evaluates each proposed action in its current context.

challenge.instructions: The task needs one input dataset and one output report but no internet. Choose the least-privilege sandbox.

choices.text: Read-only access to the input, write access to a dedicated output directory, network denied, and bounded compute.
Full home-directory and internet access with permanent credentials.
Administrator access because the plan has several steps.

challenge.explanation: It exposes exactly the resources required for the analysis while limiting exfiltration, accidental writes, and runaway computation.
hints: List concrete required resources.
Multiple steps do not imply broader authority.
Deny unused network capability.

lessons.title: Evaluate Plans under Perturbation
lessons.summary: Test goal completion, efficiency, constraint adherence, recovery, and truthful termination.

contentBlocks.text: Nominal success misses planning fragility

Replay tasks with tool timeouts, stale observations, changed resources, ambiguous goals, and partial failures. Score verified final state, policy violations, redundant actions, replanning quality, compute use, and whether the system admits incomplete work.
Long-horizon metrics
One catastrophic policy violation should not disappear inside an average success score; report severity-weighted incidents separately.

challenge.instructions: A system claims 95% completion, but state inspection verifies only 70% and finds many early stop messages. Which metric reveals the core issue?

choices.text: False completion rate against authoritative final state
Average response word count
Number of planning phrases used

challenge.explanation: The gap is between self-reported completion and verifiable world state, so termination truthfulness is the direct failure.
hints: Do not use the agent’s statement as ground truth.
Inspect actual goal predicates after execution.

courses.title: Efficient Models, Quantization & Edge AI
courses.summary: Reduce model memory and latency through quantization, calibration, cache control, batching, compilation, and device-aware deployment without hiding quality loss.

modules.title: Compression and Runtime Mechanics
modules.summary: Reason about memory traffic, numeric precision, artifact size, and representative calibration.

lessons.title: Find the Real Inference Bottleneck
lessons.summary: Distinguish compute-bound, memory-bandwidth-bound, launch-bound, and synchronization-bound workloads.

contentBlocks.text: Fewer operations do not guarantee lower latency

Autoregressive decoding often moves large weight and cache tensors for relatively little work per token, making memory bandwidth critical. Tiny kernels can instead be dominated by dispatch overhead, while prompt processing may use parallel compute efficiently.
Profile separately
Benchmark on the target backend with realistic sequence lengths. Desktop FLOP counts do not predict mobile unified-memory behavior.

challenge.instructions: Decode reads weights continuously, compute units stay idle, and lower-bit weights improve speed. Identify the likely bottleneck.
challenge.explanation: The workload is likely memory-bandwidth-bound: reducing bytes transferred per weight improves token latency even without changing the logical operation count much.
hints: The compute units are waiting.
Quantization reduced transferred bytes.
Compare arithmetic throughput with memory traffic.

lessons.title: Understand Scale, Zero Point, and Clipping
lessons.summary: Map floating values to a finite integer grid and identify its error sources.

contentBlocks.text: Quantization trades representational precision for efficiency

A scale maps integer steps to real-value intervals; an optional zero point represents real zero. Values between grid points are rounded, while values outside the calibrated range are clipped. Smaller groups adapt ranges locally but add metadata and kernels.

q = clamp(round(x / scale) + zero_point, q_min, q_max)
x_hat = scale * (q - zero_point)
Outlier channels can force a wide scale that wastes most low-bit levels on common small values. Per-channel or grouped schemes reduce this problem.

challenge.instructions: A calibrated range ends at 6, but an activation of 10 arrives. What happens in ordinary saturating quantization?

choices.text: It maps to the maximum integer level and dequantizes near 6, losing the excess.
The integer grid expands automatically without changing metadata.
It is represented exactly at every bit width.

challenge.explanation: Saturation clamps out-of-range values to the representable boundary, creating a large error for an unexpected outlier.
hints: The integer range is fixed.
Clamping occurs before dequantization.

lessons.title: Estimate Weight and Cache Memory
lessons.summary: Calculate parameter storage and add runtime overhead before claiming a model fits.

contentBlocks.text: Bit width gives a lower bound, not resident memory

Raw weight bytes equal parameter count times bits per parameter divided by eight. Group scales, tokenizer, graph buffers, temporary activations, and KV cache add overhead. Reserve memory for the operating system and application UI.

weight_bytes = parameters * bits / 8
total = weight_bytes + quant_metadata + kv_cache + workspace
Some backends unpack low-bit weights into wider buffers or duplicate mappings during load; measure peak and steady-state resident memory.

challenge.instructions: Return weight bytes plus metadata percentage and fixed runtime bytes.
challenge.starterCode:
def estimated_bytes(parameters, bits, metadata_fraction, runtime_bytes):
    weight_bytes = ____
    metadata_bytes = ____
    return ____
challenge.solution:
def estimated_bytes(parameters, bits, metadata_fraction, runtime_bytes):
    weight_bytes = parameters * bits / 8
    metadata_bytes = weight_bytes * metadata_fraction
    return weight_bytes + metadata_bytes + runtime_bytes
challenge.explanation: Parameter storage follows bit packing, metadata scales with weight bytes, and runtime allocation remains an independent additive cost.
hints: Divide total parameter bits by eight.
Multiply weight_bytes by metadata_fraction.
Add all three components.

lessons.title: Choose Post-Training or Quantization-Aware Methods
lessons.summary: Escalate compression complexity only when measured quality and hardware support justify it.

contentBlocks.text: The best numeric format is one the device accelerates

Post-training weight quantization is cheap and often a strong baseline. Activation quantization needs representative calibration. Quantization-aware training lets parameters adapt to simulated low precision but requires training data, compute, and a reliable export path.
Selection matrix
A nominal 4-bit format can be slower than 8-bit when the backend lacks optimized kernels and repeatedly dequantizes on the fly.

challenge.prompt: Compress for a supported mobile backend
challenge.instructions: Eight-bit post-training quantization meets latency but loses quality on one critical class; QAT is supported. Choose the next experiment.

choices.text: Run quantization-aware fine-tuning with representative critical-slice data and compare the same deployment artifact.
Ignore the critical class because average accuracy is stable.
Select a 2-bit format the device cannot execute.

challenge.explanation: QAT directly targets quantization robustness using supported kernels, while evaluation preserves the high-impact slice constraint.
hints: The backend path already works.
The remaining problem is quality adaptation.
Keep deployment-format evaluation identical.

lessons.title: Sample Calibration Data by Slice
lessons.summary: Fill per-slice quotas deterministically instead of calibrating on the easiest common traffic.

contentBlocks.text: Activation ranges depend on representative inputs

Calibration examples should cover realistic lengths, languages, modalities, and rare high-impact inputs. A quota sampler prevents a dominant slice from consuming the entire budget and logs shortfalls for missing coverage.

if counts[item.slice] < quotas[item.slice]:
    selected.append(item); counts[item.slice] += 1
Calibration data need not carry labels for range collection, but it must exercise the same preprocessing and model path as deployment.

challenge.prompt: Fill slice quotas in stable order
challenge.instructions: Select an item only when its slice has a positive quota not yet filled.
challenge.explanation: The per-slice counter enforces coverage limits while deterministic input order makes the chosen calibration set reproducible.
hints: Compare counts[name] with quotas[name].
Increment counts after append.
Unknown slices are already skipped.

modules.title: Cache, Batch, Deploy, and Evaluate
modules.summary: Control sequence memory, throughput, fallback, thermal behavior, and accuracy across target devices.

lessons.title: KV Cache Trades Memory for Decode Speed
lessons.summary: Understand why longer context and more concurrent sessions grow runtime memory linearly.

contentBlocks.text: Attention remembers prior keys and values

Autoregressive decoding caches key and value tensors for each layer and previous token so they are not recomputed every step. Cache size grows with layers, sequence length, key/value width, bytes per element, batch, and sometimes beam count.
cache_bytes ≈ 2 × layers × tokens × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes × batch
Grouped-query attention reduces KV heads relative to query heads, shrinking cache without changing the model’s hidden width.

challenge.instructions: Weights fit comfortably, but four simultaneous long chats trigger memory pressure. Identify a likely hidden allocation.
challenge.explanation: Per-session KV caches grow with token history and concurrency, so their combined memory can exceed the remaining headroom even when shared weights fit.
hints: Weights are shared but session state is not.
Context length multiplies cache storage.
Concurrency multiplies per-session memory.

lessons.title: Balance Continuous Batching and Latency
lessons.summary: Improve accelerator utilization without letting short requests wait behind long sequences.

contentBlocks.text: Batch composition changes every decoding step

Continuous batching inserts new requests as others finish, raising throughput. Scheduling must account for prompt length, generated tokens, cache capacity, priorities, and deadlines to avoid head-of-line blocking.
Scheduler signals
Throughput in tokens/second can improve while user time-to-first-token worsens. Optimize both with explicit service objectives.

challenge.instructions: Large offline summarization jobs saturate batches while small chat requests miss first-token targets. Choose a policy.

choices.text: Use separate priority classes or reserved capacity with starvation bounds and per-class metrics.
Always schedule the largest job first.
Report only aggregate throughput.

challenge.explanation: Priority isolation preserves interactive latency while starvation bounds and metrics keep background work progressing fairly.
hints: The workloads have different deadlines.
One throughput number hides user latency.

lessons.title: Admit Sessions within a Cache Budget
lessons.summary: Select priority-ordered sessions whose estimated KV memory fits available capacity.

contentBlocks.text: Admission control prevents mid-generation eviction storms

Estimate each session’s maximum cache footprint from current and reserved tokens. Admit highest-priority sessions that fit and defer others before allocation, leaving a safety margin for runtime workspace.

usable = capacity - safety_margin
if used + session.cache_bytes <= usable: admit(session)
Estimates should be conservative and reconciled as sessions end early; otherwise permanently reserved capacity lowers throughput.

challenge.prompt: Admit sessions by priority and memory
challenge.instructions: Sort descending priority and admit sessions that fit capacity minus safety margin.
challenge.explanation: The usable ceiling reserves workspace, and incremental used accounting prevents admitted cache estimates from exceeding it.
hints: Compare used plus cache_bytes with usable.
Increment used only after admission.
usable is already bounded below by zero.

lessons.title: Ship a Device-Tiered Model Portfolio
lessons.summary: Map hardware capability to verified artifacts, optional downloads, and honest degraded modes.

contentBlocks.text: One artifact rarely fits every edge device

Define device tiers from memory, accelerator features, OS, and sustained thermal behavior. Assign signed model variants and context caps to each tier, then retain a smaller fallback or deterministic path when installation or allocation fails.
Rollout controls
A model that runs once during launch testing may throttle badly after several minutes. Qualify sustained workloads, not only cold benchmarks.

challenge.prompt: Support older phones without cloud dependency
challenge.instructions: Choose the most honest offline-first portfolio.

choices.text: Route capable devices to verified local generative models and older devices to a bundled narrower knowledge engine with visible capability labels.
Silently upload older-device prompts despite offline mode.
Install the largest artifact everywhere and crash under memory pressure.

challenge.explanation: Tiered routing preserves offline function and transparency while respecting hardware constraints instead of changing the privacy boundary.
hints: Offline is a hard constraint.
A reduced local capability can remain useful.
Do not mislabel the active engine.

lessons.title: Evaluate the Pareto Frontier
lessons.summary: Compare quality, latency, memory, energy, size, and thermal behavior rather than declaring one model universally efficient.

contentBlocks.text: Efficiency is multi-objective

A configuration is Pareto-dominated when another is no worse on every required dimension and better on at least one. Measure cold and warm behavior, prefill and decode separately, representative quality slices, and sustained energy on each device tier.
Deployment scorecard
Quantization can change calibration, rare-token behavior, multilingual quality, and safety refusal boundaries even when average benchmark accuracy barely moves.

challenge.instructions: Variant A is faster, smaller, equally accurate on average, but sharply worse on the app’s critical multilingual slice. What is the right conclusion?

choices.text: A is not acceptable for unrestricted rollout; treat critical-slice quality as a deployment constraint.
A dominates because average accuracy is equal.
Remove multilingual inputs from monitoring.

challenge.explanation: A constraint violation on an intended critical population prevents A from dominating despite resource gains and stable aggregate quality.
hints: Pareto comparisons include required slice quality.
An average can hide a severe subgroup regression.
